The widespread online accessibility to chess has resulted in an unprecedented number of games being played, creating an ideal dataset for analyzing the game's structure through various statistical and information-theoretic approaches. Leveraging PGN files downloaded from Chess.com platforms, which comprise nearly a billion games, we provide an in-depth analysis of the most common opening sequences and their evolution over time. Key metrics such as the frequency of specific moves, moves within sequences, and entire opening methods are examined, revealing remarkable similarities between White and Black moves and significant correlations in move and opening probabilities. Additionally, we calculate and compare the complexity of different openings, finding distinct patterns of move and opening probabilities for both colors. Our investigation also explores the relationship between observed frequencies and theoretical predictions for specific moves, sequences, and entire openings, with white pieces showing higher degrees of unpredictability compared to their black counterparts.

This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse.

A method to derive constants of motion beyond local bounds for ODE-based Lagrangian systems is outlined, including a practical example that illustrates its utility for dissipative mechanical systems and its implications on solution existence and behavior under specific assumptions. The framework is further extended to cover Euler-Lagrange equations with order greater than two, yielding new first integrals for particular models, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, paving the way for potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future.

Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Nonetheless, effective methods for finding 2D sketches in 3D contexts have been absent. In this work, we address a novel task - creating a query from a 3D VR sketch and using it for 3D retrieval. Our proposed approach involves generating an implicit implicitation from the VR sketch and extracting features from it, which then facilitate 3D retrieval. Importantly, our approach does not necessitate any training. For testing purposes, we developed the WorldSketch v1 dataset, comprising manual sketches in both explicit and implicit formats, as well as open-source applications for creating explicit sketches on a tablet and converting them to implicit drawings. Furthermore, we propose a retrieval method that leverages our extracted features, and our approach demonstrates superior 3D retrieval results on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

HD80606b, a planet with a very short 1-month orbit around its host star, undergoes a dramatic temperature change from 500K to 1500K as it moves from the outer regions inward and then far away again. Because of this extreme temperature fluctuation, it is an ideal candidate for studying the atmosphere of close-orbiting planets with advanced space telescopes. In order to maximize the scientific output from the James Webb Space Telescope, it is necessary to accurately predict HD80606b's position and movement. Utilizing multiple years of photometric and spectrometric observations with the Infrared Telescope in space and the support of the Kepler mission, we have made substantial advancements in understanding the planet's orbit. By analyzing its orbital period and movement patterns, we have created a more accurate model that can be verified through further observations. In addition to its periodic motion, we have taken into account the precession of its orbit due to the influence of the host star's gravitational pull on other nearby objects.

In this investigation, we're looking at how a specific type of matter collapse, governed by a certain relationship between pressure and density, behaves under the assumption that the matter doesn't heat up as it collapses. We found that, similar to a previously studied case with constant temperature, this relationship doesn't consistently describe a thermodynamically valid process. However, by making the relationship between pressure and density more complex, we were able to identify conditions under which the matter's behavior remains thermodynamically valid. These conditions led to two possible scenarios: the first is that the mass of the matter must be above a certain minimum threshold to prevent the matter from becoming unstable as it collapses to the center; the second is that the matter's temperature must rise significantly, potentially exceeding any initial temperature, under specific conditions related to the distribution of the matter. In both cases, the matter's temperature behavior changes dramatically when it becomes very dense, resulting in the matter becoming potentially unstable again.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality conditions of any four-dimensional black hole. Our approach involves introducing a family of one-parameter solutions and applying the first variation with respect to this parameter. For the specific case of the Riemannian formulation, our results align with previously published findings. However, our approach offers the distinct advantage of generalizability to black holes that do not possess a specific vector field structure.

A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome distribution, known as end-effect exploration, to find a policy that efficiently achieves this objective. Current approaches utilizing reward functions as influences on this objective distribution often struggle due to unreliable data and slow convergence. In contrast, our approach directly optimizes the policy to match the target outcome distribution, utilizing end-effect drives that simplify this optimization. We enhance the efficiency of end-effect drives by integrating them with end-effect exploration, resulting in improved resource usage and faster end-effect drive convergence. Additionally, our approach leads to better final performance with more consistent outcomes, specifically when combining end-effect exploration with end-effect drives shows superior results in achieving optimal resource constraints and meeting the target outcome distribution.

A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour and features a Fierz-Ginocchio type structure in its R-matrix. The R-matrix's properties are influenced by a parameter p, and when p equals three, it matches the characteristics of a 3-colour SU(3) system. We have derived the key features of a 3D gravity and matter theory that conforms to this generalized Poincaré algebra. Our findings include explicit expressions for the 3D metric and gauge fields in terms of their dynamical variables. Additionally, we have confirmed that the newly discovered system can be transformed into second-class constraints through second-class constraints.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm dependent on the source degree, and a fixed-parameter algorithm reliant on the source degree exponent. Our novel methods combine bounded independence and treewidth techniques, and we've overcome existing barriers by introducing a new structural concept of nearly tree-like complexity.

Effectively choosing past experiences to facilitate navigation in unfamiliar environments is crucial for human cognition. However, most selected memories may not be beneficial for navigation, leading to unnecessary consumption of computational resources. To address this, we propose MemoNav, a novel framework that strategically selects relevant memories during training to facilitate navigation. By distinguishing significant from insignificant memories, MemoNav categorizes them, selects the relevant ones, and trains a model to distinguish informative memories, resulting in reduced training time and improved memory selection accuracy. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that MemoNav can distinguish relevant memories, accelerates convergence, and yields superior navigation performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

To enhance cellular coverage and flexibility, operators have deployed small cells as necessary supplements to macro cells within the 4G and 5G networks. Although initial deployments were primarily driven by data traffic requirements, upcoming 5G-Advanced and 6G technologies are expected to bring about a paradigm shift in the role of small cells. These future networks will demand unprecedented coverage and connectivity, necessitating the development of innovative small cell solutions that leverage emerging technologies such as terahertz, intelligent surfaces, and integrated sensing and communication. This article explores the characteristics of traditional small cells, identifies challenges that need to be addressed in future networks, and proposes innovative small cell models that can meet these challenges and meet the requirements of future high-density, high-data traffic environments.

We've developed a comprehensive framework to model complex interactions between multiple entangled systems using hypergraphs. This approach can be applied to several processes and we'll specifically explore how certain conditions lead to spontaneous pattern emergence in systems where individual units interact with each other. Our focus will be on two specific settings: one involving interactions between groups over long distances, and another with diffusive interactions between units. Additionally, we'll demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through applications to both the generalized Volterra system and the Brusselator model.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems, a characteristic of systems like those with 1D Chern-Simney theory. We establish that in such systems, the entanglement of evolved operators grows linearly when duals are taken duals in momentum space. Specifically, we take the dual of a spatially expanding Fermi hole and discover an accompanying dual, temporal Holevo entanglement growth. Employing the framework of out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs), we show the Holevo metric captures a comprehensive picture of entanglement among time-evolved creation and annihilation operators, thus demonstrating operator four-way growth. We demonstrate one-way growth of both the Fermi-Dirac and Bose- Einstein distributions in both fermionic and bosonic cases, respectively.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of 12  helium-4 nuclei  in  an  excited  state  of  carbon-12,  plays  a  crucial  role  in  determining  the  rate  of  nuclear  reactions  vital  to  stellar  evolution  and  cosmological carbon abundance. Recent studies using advanced simulations indicate that interactions within the  helium-4 nuclei  in  the  Hoyle  state  are  influenced  by  short-range  forces,  which  may  affect  the  rate  of  carbon-12 formation. To investigate this phenomenon, researchers conducted an experiment using the  STARA  beam  at  FRM-II  to  measure  the  probability  of  carbon-12  formation  directly  from  an  intermediate  state,  avoiding  complications  arising  from  competing  reactions.  The  results  of  this  measurement  reveal that the influence of short-range forces on the  helium-4 nuclei  in  the  Hoyle  state  likely enhance the  carbon-12  formation  rate  by  up  to  10  percent,  which  could  have  significant  implications  for  our  understanding  of  stellar evolution.

We investigate the dynamics of cracks in two-dimensional linear elastic materials. The model accounts for two inherent properties - a minimum time and a length scale - that dictate the maximum speed of the crack's propagation. The study demonstrates that an elastic material's minimum time and length properties determine a critical speed for the transition from stable to unstable crack growth. When the elastic time and length properties diverge from their minimum values, this critical speed increases significantly. Both theoretical analysis using singularity theory and extensive computational simulations via a discrete dislocation model reveal that crack propagation becomes oscillatory beyond a certain speed. This behavior manifests as a phenomenon known as "beating," characterized by self-sustained oscillations in energy release rates, that emerges abruptly at the critical threshold. The shape of this oscillation, however, varies gradually with increasing distance from the critical threshold. This 20,000-word review encompasses crack dynamics, material properties, and fracture patterns in two-dimensional systems.

In a general finite-state information channel with feedback and with state, it's often impossible to determine capacity exactly. However, when the channel follows a Markov process and the encoder has access to this state, it has been proven that a finite machine can achieve the maximum mutual information possible, provided that this machine remains stable under the combined influence of its own and the channel's transitions. In cases where the system is stable, this achievement can be attained by a device similar to a one-tap equalizer, making it possible to establish an upper limit for the original problem. Additionally, this achievement also enables one to establish a one-tap equalizer similar theorem for the related erasure channel with memory and feedback.

A novel class of superconductors, known as topological superconductors, has significant implications in the field due to the presence of Majorana fermions at their edges. Theoretically, it has been proposed that certain materials with strong spin-orbit coupling can host truly topological superconductivity in the absence of external influences. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers have utilized the attractive Rashba Hubbard model as a theoretical framework to describe the pairing of opposite-spin electrons due to Rashba spin-orbit coupling alone. Through the application of the variational Monte Carlo method, they found evidence of short-range topological superconducting properties in the ground state of this model, and recently, they found an increase in the transition temperature of the system with the strength of the spin-orbit coupling.

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare cell information effectively. To address this challenge, we introduced a new dataset for SemEval 2020 Task 9: SEM-TAB-FACTS, aiming to verify factual information and locate supporting evidence within tabular scientific data. The comprehensive dataset contains 1,363 sentences supplemented by an additional development set of 200 sentences. Our team participated in both the Sub-Task A (Verdict Prediction) and Sub-Task B (Evidence Finding) competitions of SEM-TAB-FACTS. We achieved an accuracy rate of 75.0% and F1 scores of 73.9 (Start Cell), 70.2 (End Cell), and 74.3 (Table ID) on the table-related evidence finding sub-tasks. For Verdict Prediction, our model attained an accuracy rate of 75.0%.

This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely. The smallest size of such a subset that does this across all graphs is known as the metric dimension. We've defined a variation of this concept where the unique pointers from the subset can accurately determine the distance between a vertex and a point in the graph up to a certain limit k, which gives us the idea of k-identifiable sets and their dimension. We've investigated this new dimension in various graph types such as paths, cycles, trees, and others, calculating its value in these instances and exploring how it behaves under certain graph operations for these families.

This work explores the potential of integrating an ozone O3 and ultraviolet (UV) light system for effectively eliminating pollutants in flue gas emissions. A numerical model of the UV unit and an ozone unit have been developed. In the UV unit, solid SO3 is formed on the walls of the reaction chamber from gas phase SO2 using UV radiation, accompanied by the generation of O2 and water vapor. An upstream ozone unit is employed to supply the necessary O3 for the reaction. N2, SO2, H2O, and O2 concentrations within the reaction chamber are analyzed. It has been demonstrated that varying UV lamp power and flow rate can optimize SO3 conversion. Utilizing UV lamps with higher power and lower flow rates results in optimal O2 and SO3 conversion in flue gas. Furthermore, maintaining a low water concentration in the reaction chamber can prevent erosion on glass walls and mitigate corrosion risks associated with SO3.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Testing neural network applications on simulated neuromorphic systems requires significant computational power, which can be addressed by leveraging the parallel capabilities of host systems. By utilizing Virtual Private Clouds, the host system's unused processing units can be harnessed. In this context, Model-in-Loop co-design simulations, involving SystemC templates and custom-built neural workloads, constitute critical benchmarks. By distributing these simulations across a cluster of computing units via the VPC's network, the load can be optimized and scaled efficiently, as demonstrated by the runtime comparisons between local and distributed simulations on six computing units within an AWS cloud environment.

Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges,
mainly stemming from uninterpretable models, questionable reliance on imperfect
data, or offering a sole prediction outcome without considering various
probability outcomes.
  This study proposes the concept of Indecision Trees as a novel and adaptable
extension of the existing Decision Tree model. These models are designed to
effectively handle multiple prediction probabilities, offer clear reasoning for
their conclusions, and are easy to understand due to their interpretable nature.
  To develop Indecision Tree models, we integrate the ideas of decision theory,
quantified uncertainty, and first-order logic. This integration enables the
distinguishing of reliable and unreliable data points, and our analysis reveals
that the resulting Indecision Tree models maintain a strong level of
mathematical rigor. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of
Indecision Tree models on three different datasets, outperforming their
traditional counterparts and achieving a balance between accuracy and
interpretability.

The DTW distance is frequently applied to sequence comparison in various fields,
but its time complexity hinders its scalability. To address this challenge, we
propose an efficient DTW distance calculation method called PrunedDTW, which time-
limits the trajectory of the DTW distance calculation, thereby enhancing its
efficiency. However, this time constraint may result in inaccurate distance
estimates due to premature termination, an issue we address through a novel
algorithm, Early Abandoning PrunedDTW, which limits the search path, and proposes
a new distance calculation metric based on DTW, DTTW, to accelerate the
trajectory of DTW distance calculation, ultimately improving its efficiency. We
evaluate EAPrunedDTW, which integrates the proposed solution with PrunedDTW, in
the context of similarity search and demonstrate its superior performance over
the original PrunedDTW, and the differences in calculation paths of DTW, and
PrunedDTW.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights or highlight specific differences in test cases and faults. However, there is no research exploring the effectiveness of inquiry-based learning methods in teaching testing concepts through the framework of MuSE. Our study introduces a new inquiry-based approach using a semantic similarity metric, and evaluates its effectiveness against traditional feedback methods. The investigation involves an experiment with 90 undergraduate students from an introductory software testing course. The results show that the proposed inquiry-based method is capable of teaching testing concepts, and is similar in efficiency to traditional feedback, although it may take slightly longer to achieve comparable learning outcomes.

In this study, we merge two research fields, specifically concept analysis and rule learning from machine teaching, along with Conjecture Analysis, to create a new approach for generating explanations in machine learning. Our analysis reveals that current definition-based and feature-based explanations share underlying similarities, leading us to introduce the framework of explanatory learning. We focus on demonstrative explanations, encompassing both their concepts and features. We propose a framework for learning these explanatory patterns using inductive logic programming, which accommodates both concepts and features. Our framework leverages the advantages of proposition learning logic programming and Prolog's feature matching capabilities. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our framework in producing explanatory patterns. Our implementation, named Conceptual Rule Learning, includes concepts, features, and the ability to learn correlations. Our framework exhibits superior performance, both theoretically and empirically, compared to existing rule learning methods, specifically differentiable rule learning and attention-based rule learning.

Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause and its implications. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon is presented in this article, delving into the mathematical underpinnings of how high-order Graph Convolutional Networks are calculated. The study reveals that the integration of higher-order calculations in Graph Convolutional Networks amplifies the impact of leaf node features, rendering them synonymous with the graph's root node features. As a consequence, critical local differentiation information is lost, leading to the over-smoothing effect. Based on this finding, the article proposes modified Graph Convolutional Network formulations to mitigate the over-smoothing issue, demonstrating enhanced performance in classification tasks.

Dark matter particles interacting via force mediation are sought after in proton-proton collisions at the CMS experiment at the CERN LHC, specifically those accompanied by a leptonally decaying Z boson. Between 2016 and 2018, data collected at a luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ with center-of-mass energies of 13 TeV were examined. To isolate these events, selections based on high momentum, missing transverse momentum, and additional jet activity were applied. Comparing simulated outcomes with measured data across various channels, no significant signs of new particles were found, leading to upper limits on dark matter production rates. Furthermore, this data conforming to the Standard Model resulted in exclusion regions being set for dark matter parameters including the momentum threshold for production, the nature of the force mediator, and characteristics of the final state particles.

We propose a new set of functions that depend on transverse momentum to describe the distribution of quarks and gluons within hadrons, which are denoted as $F_{\iota_1\cdots\iota_n|j}^{(n, j-1, j)}(k_T^2)$, with additional constraints from the first moment of conventional parton distribution functions for $n \leq 2$, this model is further guided by the anomalous dimensions within the standard PDFs framework. Beyond its relevance to Sivers, twist-3, and Boer-Mulders, or twist-2 $k_T$-dependent functions descriptions, this model has broader implications for the formulation of T-odd transverse momentum-dependent distribution functions as well as for LHC parton flux analysis. This framework's flexibility and extensions are explored including multi-parton Fock states and anomalous dimensions.

Homeomorphisms with compact support on a Tychonoff space can be given several equivalent topological structures by viewing them as either a union of groups of homeomorphisms with the same support size or as a subset of the group of homeomorphisms of its compactified space. A space has the CSHP if these two definitions yield the same topological space, which is the main topic of the paper's methods to prove that product spaces of specific spaces with CSHP possess CSHP.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene has shown that it enables the growth of crystalline films on amorphous substrates with a reduced substrate influence. Nevertheless, direct experiments on multi-component Heusler alloys have not been conducted to date, largely due to their inherently complex atomic structure. Consequently, this study investigates the details of remote epitaxy on graphene for a Heusler alloy with a simple structure, CrMnSb. Notably, this study reveals that remote epitaxy is not universally applicable even when the bulk material exhibits a perfect lattice match. Furthermore, it has been discovered that, when the lattice match deteriorates, the growth mechanism shifts to a remnant epitaxy derived from the underlying substrate via the graphene layer. At an even lower lattice match, the growth mechanism transitions to vapor-liquid-solid epitaxy, characterized by prolonged incubation periods. These findings emphasize that epitaxial behavior in remote epitaxy is highly dependent on specific atomic structures and is not solely governed by bulk properties, thus highlighting a highly versatile method for exploring this phenomenon across a wide range of materials.

We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large sets of time series data, even when the relationships change over time and the data contains extreme values. A new method is proposed that can automatically adjust for varying levels of dependence and the probability of extreme values. A novel approach based on the change in probability of extreme events is used to determine the relationship and probability of extreme values, which can then be used to make accurate estimates. Theoretical analysis confirms how the method converges and that the estimates are robust to errors in assumption. This is demonstrated through simulations and the examination of real data that predicts changes in US stock markets.

Recent JWST observations of El Gordo (ACT-CL J0102-4915), the second strongest galaxy cluster found in the universe, revealed four distinct arcs and numerous background galaxies.  Using HST, ELVIS, and JWST observations, along with a Bayesian prior based on the mass distribution of similar galaxy clusters, we developed an advanced lens model to accurately predict the shape of 17 selected background galaxies.  The model found that El Gordo's two main clusters, the North and South Clusters, have different levels of influence on the observed arcs and that the forward collision of these clusters is further along than previously thought.  Furthermore, the model identified a remarkable galaxy in the Northern Cluster with a redshift of 2.934, and with a estimated mass of 2.4 x 109 to 1.6 x 1011 solar masses.  This discovery is significant because it sheds light on the evolution of galaxy clusters and the formation of galaxies.  The data also indicates that El Gordo will eventually settle as a typical galaxy cluster following forward collision.  The far-infrared light from this massive galaxy in the eastern arc was measured by JWST and is located behind a distorted image in the Northern Cluster.  The model suggests that the intrinsic shape of this red and round source is small, and that it could be a red supergiant star like Betelgeuse but located at a far distance in

Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards improving network infrastructure, with promises of better Quality of Service. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the Content Provider agreeing to a portion of the profits, and the ISPs competing for Content Provider's traffic through targeted pricing. We reveal that profit-sharing agreements lead to improved pricing strategies among Content and Service Providers compared to scenarios without such agreements, where a portion of Content Providers' profits is kept as revenue, leading to increased efficiency and potential for both parties to benefit in the long run.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through a mathematical framework that relates these concepts through an adjoint relationship.

The $\alpha$-attractor models in inflationary theory hold great promise in the context of the tensor mode signature, particularly due to their simplicity in the model's structure. Prior research typically relied on specific $\alpha$-attractor models, such as the logarithmic $\alpha$-attractor model, to define the trajectory of scalar field evolution, and compared their predictions against data from the Planck collaboration and future space-based initiatives like the LiteBIRD project. In contrast, this study adopts a more comprehensive approach by examining various $\alpha$-attractor models that could potentially align with current cosmological data and outlines their associated predictions for tensor modes. Specifically, we analyze over 10000000000 potential logarithmic, power-law, and trigonometric $\alpha$-attractor models in a standard Einstein gravity framework to determine their corresponding field trajectory, model parameters, and resulting predictions for tensor modes. Our investigation reveals that the logarithmic $\alpha$-attractor model, with an associated power of $\beta$ ranging from approximately $0.04$ to $0.20$, is consistent with current data, while the trigonometric model allows for a broader range of $\beta$ values, extending up to the order of one. Furthermore, we identify specific predictions for tensor modes associated with these models, and our analysis suggests that the $\alpha$-attractor models, particularly the logarithmic and trigonometric variants, are capable

In the context of a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic three-dimensional manifold with a boundary that approaches infinity, its foliations measured at infinity directly relate to the horizontal measured foliations derived from the uniformization maps associated with its components that extend towards infinity. For a given hyperbolic surface that a pair of measured foliations, denoted by $\mathsf{F}_+$ and $\mathsf{F}_-$, relates to a hyperbolic three-dimensional manifold that extends towards infinity, our main theorem states that there exists a way to adjust the parameters called the "complex structures" within the space corresponding to these surface types to result in a representation that extends towards infinity that pairs with the given pair of foliations. Moreover, this theorem also confirms the existence and uniqueness (except under specific circumstances) of this association. Building upon this, a corollary is revealed: for any given hyperbolic surface, there exists a way to pair the set containing its two associated foliations with the given pair of foliations. Furthermore, these two theorems have important implications for understanding the relationship between the space representing deformations and topological transformations of these surface types.

This study examines the cross-sectional distribution of portfolio returns, derived from the underlying cross-sectional distribution of individual asset returns and the specific portfolio weights assigned. By the application of large deviation theory, return extremes in each portfolio can be extremal within their individual asset returns, resulting in distinctive and measurable portfolio returns. Specifically, notable returns in each portfolio can significantly influence the overall market, under certain conditions. Moreover, this analysis reveals that the impact of a particular portfolio on the market is contingent upon the concentration of its weights. This insight provides the theoretical foundation for emerging portfolios characterized by diverse applications and unique structures.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate listening to heart sounds can be hampered by background noise and other distortions, which vary depending on where the stethoscope is placed. To improve the accuracy of hearing the heart, researchers are using deep learning methods to analyze cardiac sounds, but current methods often require large amounts of data enhanced with unrealistic amounts of background noise. To address this, the authors of this paper propose a new method that accurately enhances background noise and artificially changes the cardiac signal to replicate the effects of real-world listening conditions. Additionally, the proposed method uses a two-network approach to better handle the challenges of point-of-care listening scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in enhancing the performance of existing heart sound classifiers under difficult listening conditions.

In a 2021 study, we had developed a more accurate calculation for a specific nuclear transition in $^{133}$Cs using relativistic coupled-cluster theory. Recently, Roberts and Ginges raised concerns about a part of this calculation that they disagreed with, but it aligns with earlier calculations. In response, we thoroughly justify our method and highlight that all components were treated equally, addressing the concerns raised by the critics, $[{\rm Phys.\ Rev.\ Lett.\ {\bf 127}, 141602 (2021)]$, while also thanking them for their positive feedback.

A twist is utilized to analyze families of algebraic varieties, with equiva lant twists under the action of a group G investigated in this study. A comprehensive list of unique varieties exists, resulting from twists of an algebraic variety X, which are equi valent under the action of G. Focusing on twists of algebraic varieties, with al terations on the torus, we examine equi valence here. By allowing G to be 2-Dimensional crystallographic point groups, we establish a relationship with 2-Dimensional families of Riccati Equations.

Pomona College's Mathematics & Statistics Department has been dedicated to
establishing an inclusive and welcoming environment for all students to
engage in mathematical study. In response to low diversity among majors, the
department initially attempted to address this through targeted programs aimed
at enhancing students' mathematical abilities. Conversely, recent efforts have
shifted to an anti-deficit strategy, which prioritizes modifying the
department's internal culture to foster a more cohesive community. Our
initiatives to boost collaboration, atmosphere, and overall department
climate are detailed below.

We examine the boundedness of the fractional series operator $T_{\gamma}$, with its given function form $(T_{\gamma}b)(j)$, in the discrete $H^{p}(w)$ spaces, where $p$ lies between $1$ and $2$ and $w$ is an A$_{2}$ Muckenhoupt weight. The operator $T_{\gamma}$ is defined for $\gamma$ values greater than $0$ and $p$ values greater than $\gamma$. Our study demonstrates that even when this condition is not met, i.e., $0$ is less than or equal to $\gamma$ and it is less than or equal to $p$ and $p$ is less than or equal to $2$, the operator $T_{\gamma}$ remains bounded on discrete $H^{p}(w)$ spaces, provided that this weight is well-defined. Furthermore, we explore the end-point boundedness, specifically the case of $p$ being equal to $1$ of the operator $T_{\gamma}$ on discrete $H^{p}(w)$ spaces, where $w$ is a well-defined A$_{1}$ weight, and we derive specific examples of $T_{\gamma}$ being bounded on discrete $H^{p}(w)$ and $H^{p}_{\sigma}$ spaces.

This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and overall auction results. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants compete in second-price auctions with simulated agents, we investigate whether a seller's credibility in committing to not retract their bid bid impacts bidding tactics and prices. Our findings indicate that when the seller's integrity is present, it can increase prices above standard expectations in second-price auctions, validating economic theories that assume irrational bidder behavior in certain auction circumstances. Moreover, we observe a significant difference in bidding tactics and prices when the seller's integrity is absent versus present, providing clear evidence of a link between auction format integrity and both bidding tactics and overall auction results.

The explanation for the long-standing discrepancy between predicted and predicted universe uniformity can be found in the modified gravitational framework called $f(Q)$, where the parameter $n$ has a value greater than $2$. Investigating the universe's early development using the isotropic, locally rotationally symmetric Bianchi-I model reveals how it gradually became uniform. Within this model, we examine various characteristics of the early universe, such as energy density, pressure, geometric quantities, and the Hubble parameter. Based on this analysis, we show how the model's anisotropic nature fades and it aligns with the isotropic Friedmann-Robertson-Walker universe when coupled with the $f(Q)$ theory of gravity. We also discuss what implications this has for the universe's evolution.

We initiate a study of local defining ideals of Hessenberg varieties, specifically focusing on regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A, utilizing an affine coordinate chart known as the Geometric Vertex Decomposition. By analyzing these ideals, we demonstrate that they constitute a Gröbner basis with respect to the Plücker embedding, derived from regular nilpotent Hessenberg subvarieties, which inherit their defining ideals from the Plücker coordinates. Furthermore, we provide a method of splitting the Frobenius on the Hessenberg varieties, justified combinatorially, that reflects the combinatorial properties of subvarieties, and finally, we illustrate the duality between defining ideals and subvarieties, linking them to the fixed point variety of the Lagrangian Grassmannian under the action of the symplectic group.

Neural Painters, utilizing a GAN-based approach, generate brushstrokes that are assembled into paintings. Despite GANs' superiority in AI-generated art, their training can be exceptionally challenging. To address these difficulties and accelerate Neural Painter training, we employed Transfer Learning, achieving a notable time reduction from days to just hours without compromising visual quality. Our findings are presented in this study.

We tackle current issues with the flavor anomalies in the $K$ and $B$ mesons, incorporating the V$_u$ anomaly and a new symmetry, Vb, by proposing compositeness, with with possible exceptions e and light quarks. Our proposed model addresses the V$_u$ and Vb anomalies, reduces $K$ mixing constraints, and accounts for the $B \to K \nu \bar{\nu}$ anomaly, however the diphoton anomaly is addressed by altering Higgs couplings.

We introduce a new dataset consisting of 2,599 information-seeking questions, which we've incorporated along with their answers from academic papers. This dataset aims to tackle information retrieval challenges within the domain of research papers. A brief overview of our dataset, along with the underlying motivations, is presented here, followed by additional information as per our supplementary material. This work was undertaken as part of the D2-RL project.

In 3D core-collapse supernovae, under specific circumstances, neutrino flavors can rapidly change within regions near the collapsing core. This process is influenced by the magnetic fields and high-density environment surrounding the protoneutron star. A study was conducted to investigate the physical properties and mathematical description of this rapid flavor transformation. It was observed that when two adjacent regions have unequal lepton number densities, rapid flavor transformation occurs at their intersection, leading to an increase in electron neutrinos. This research also found that the energy released from this process causes the area involved to expand, leading to rapid flavor instability. It was noted that the rate of this transformation is primarily influenced by two factors: the difference in electron number densities and the MNSR parameter, which represents the minimum value of the product of the neutrino and antineutrino number densities. It was found that the frequency of this rapid flavor transformation is directly related to the number density and MNSR parameter. Additionally, it was observed that the anisotropic velocity fields within the protoneutron star significantly impact the system's behavior, causing the areas involved to change size and thereby affecting the rate of this process. This change in size can lead to a transition between and within islands of undressed and dressed quasiclassical states.

ADHD is a widely prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder that is often difficult to diagnose due to its overlapping symptoms. Advances in imaging technology have allowed researchers to identify abnormalities in specific brain regions of individuals with ADHD using resting-state fMRI. The field of ADHD diagnosis using Machine Learning is burgeoning, yet to date, no study has attempted to pinpoint crucial regions of the brain for training a deep learning model to diagnose ADHD more effectively. By applying a Deep Zoom model to analyze rs-fMRI data, we discovered that enhancing the spatial resolution and incorporating spatial information significantly boosts diagnostic accuracy. Furthermore, by developing a marker-based model that emphasizes the probability maps of relevant brain areas, we found that distilling the protocol data to just the parietal and prefrontal lobes significantly improves ADHD diagnosis through a deep learning model.

In a discrete-time epidemic SISI model where population growth is constant and balanced, the per capita mortality and fertility rates are equivalent, and the model's evolution operator is a nonlinear function of seven parameters. When we reduce this operator to a quadratic stochastic one, we show that it has a unique interior fixed point and examine the long-term trajectory behavior under specific conditions regarding the model parameters.

Acronyms and abbreviations share similarities, but they differ in application and context. Acronyms form new words, often capitalized, serving as standalone entries in dictionaries, whereas abbreviations retain the original words they represent, typically appearing in lowercase. Despite their overlap, current NLP tools and resources focus on identifying and categorizing all acronym and abbreviation instances, rather than distinguishing between the two. Acronym and abbreviation disambiguation presents additional challenges, but can be made more manageable by incorporating a simple indicator to differentiate between them, which our proposed model leverages to improve performance and efficiency. Introducing a classification step enables the development of more specialized tools and diverse knowledge bases, specifically aimed at disambiguating acronyms and abbreviations separately. Additionally, during indicator identification, the structure of potential acronyms and abbreviations is validated, facilitating the enhancement of indicator models and abbreviation/acronym identification through self-correction mechanisms. While a simple rule-based approach has shown to significantly boost performance, a more sophisticated machine learning-based model has also been explored and can serve as a versatile component for acronym/abbreviation/indicator identification tasks.

Heat conduction through a quantum Hall junction can be controlled by dividing the geometric mean of the applied heat currents by the temperature difference across the junction. This is possible due to the heat current interference at the junction, which is regulated by the phase differences in the wave functions of the incoming electrons. By adjusting the magnetic field, this linear relationship between heat currents and temperature can be reversed, and the temperature coefficient of the voltage response at the junction can be modified up to 100%. This effect is demonstrated numerically, and it is shown that this interference-driven switching and heat rectification can be amplified and made more robust with the use of multiple arms in the junction.

Our research focuses on improving file organization within DNA-based object databases, specifically addressing the need for hierarchical object structures and update capabilities without excessive redundancy.  To this end, we've developed the DH storage scheme, which enables flexible directory hierarchies and efficient file updates while optimizing DNA sequence lengths.  Moreover, a proposed hierarchy-homomorphic scheme allows for simplified object structures, and a new evaluation metric is introduced to better assess hierarchy-related DNA costs.  Using a real-world dataset, we demonstrate that our scheme strikes a balance between practical data management requirements and computational efficiency, yielding a 61.6% reduction in DNA sequence lengths when handling scattered large files, and a 98.8% decrease in the frequency of large files requiring complete rewriting.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and robust transport of charges or signals. Researchers have successfully realized various types of topological insulators through photonic applications, where exceptional properties of momentum space nodal lines in these applications lead to fascinating outcomes. One such property is the non-trivial topological index, specifically the Zak phase, linked to geometric phases and related to the winding number at nodal lines in momentum space. In this context, researchers explore the relationship between topological insulators and nodal lines in momentum space, considering models like the Dirac and Weyl points as examples. Dirac points represent the intersection of multiple bands at a singular energy level, while Weyl points represent the crossing of multiple bands at singular locations in momentum space. Researchers discuss the topological characteristics of these models and their real-world applications, such as charge separation in the Dirac charge pump. Furthermore, the robustness of photonic applications based on nodal lines in momentum space is ensured by the geometric properties at Weyl points, which prevent backscattering and enhance the stability of momentum and direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of direction of

In oscillatory systems that feature both slow and fast variables, the interaction between them significantly impacts the overall dynamics. When the system exhibits a stable oscillation in the smaller variable, introducing a second, self-sustaining oscillation leads to complex interactions between the two modes. These interactions give rise to pacemaker-generated waves when boundary conditions cause the advection of these modes through the system, resulting in a phenomenon known as boundary phase modulation. Research has shown that the advection of these modes can overtake the oscillations' natural frequencies, producing traveling waves that originate from the boundary. This study presents two mathematical models, one a simplified version of the Gray–Scott system and a more complex adaptation of the Fitzhugh-Nagumo equations, to better understand the factors governing these waves' speed. By analyzing these models and comparing them to a more comprehensive numerical simulation, two approximate formulas have been developed to predict the waves' speed with remarkable accuracy, thereby offering a simplified approach to predicting wave behavior in the field of reaction-diffusion systems.

A fundamental concept, entropy, has significant implications in both classical and quantum physics, and it directly influences the performance of a wide range of applications, spanning communication systems to machine learning algorithms. Recent research focused on approximating entropy to a multiplicative margin within quantum frameworks, resulting in bounds ranging from exponential to near constant, depending on the type of entropy and purity, respectively. This paper contributes a novel method for estimating the entropy of an arbitrary quantum state in polynomial time, relative to the purity of the state, and improves previous approaches by enabling approximate entropy calculation with a lower query complexity for states with positive purity values. Additionally, the paper introduces an algorithm to determine the Renyi entropy for quantum systems, under specific conditions where the R\'enyi parameter is greater than one, with the attained bound being near-optimal according to a specific lower bound.

Implementing and deploying effective artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, necessitates substantial datasets for training, testing, and validation processes. Establishing comprehensive data collections, annotated in accordance with standardized protocols, necessitates the setup of imaging biobanks, which involves meticulous data management and computational infrastructure to facilitate training, Annotated image data, and reporting. To tackle these complexities, meticulous planning and the development of a robust, scalable data management system, as well as high-performance computing facilities, are indispensable. This chapter delves into the complexities of data collection, storage solutions, and the utilization of cloud-based and on-premise computing resources to execute AI pipelines, emphasizing the importance of scalability, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness to ensure successful AI implementation.

Physicians' written assessments, known as problem lists, contain crucial information about patients' conditions formatted in unstructured text. To streamline clinical workflows and reduce errors, physicians rely on electronic health record systems. Interim National Disease Classification guidelines, created by clinicians and coders, standardize condition descriptions but require manual input, leading to inaccuracies and delays. A proposed method using semi-self-supervised learning efficiently trains a condition extraction model with minimal annotations by leveraging minimal description transformations and maximal agreement, outperforming traditional supervised learning approaches. Compared to existing automated coding systems, this method surpasses them while offering new insights into patients' conditions, as evidenced by experiments on a real-world dataset with 1.3M NDCG codes.

Let $R$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field $k$. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is considered almost Cohen-Macaulay if its local cohomology modules share the same vector space dimensions as those of a Cohen-Macaulay ideal in the given conditions. This research explores nearly Cohen-Macaulay monomial ideals and identifies specific classes of these ideals within the given ring structure. Additionally, several examples are provided to illustrate almost Cohen-Macaulay monomial ideals and their properties.

Due to their unique properties, quantum machines have the potential to outperform traditional computers, particularly in tasks like pattern recognition. This crucial ability encompasses both unsupervised learning (finding inherent structure in data) and supervised learning (using labeled data to make predictions). This tutorial introduces the fundamental concepts of quantum computing and explores both unsupervised and supervised methods applicable to quantum machines. Specifically, we discuss how to adapt popular machine learning techniques to quantum processors, and highlight emerging approaches designed to exploit the specific capabilities of superconducting qubit-based devices.

Our analysis of 178 variable stars, discovered in prime fields during 2018 by the KMTNet network, yielded 11 anomalies potentially indicative of exoplanets, based on microlensing data. These objects were examined using the anomaly finite source method (AFFS), a novel approach that doesn't rely on the lensing effect. We found that our sample of 178 objects in 2018 included the following anomalies: ten objects displaying self-lensings, driven by the passage of a stellar companion across the path of a primary source star, yet unaffected by the passage of smaller substructures; one object exhibiting a self-lensing effect from a dense object such as a brown dwarf or star, which lenses the light of a primary source; and one object displaying a complex, mixed signal consisting of both a self-lensing effect and a gravitational wave, which may indicate the presence of a dark matter clump or a planetary object. Our results suggest that the 2018 prime-field sample may contain fewer planetary objects than expected, and that the prime-field strategy of searching for planetary objects in areas of the sky that are difficult to access may not be as effective as the romfield strategy of searching for planetary objects in areas of the sky that are easy to access.

Finding solutions to inverse problems in computer vision relies on an advanced version of gradient descent called the gradient descent optimization (GDO), which requires access to accurate gradients of complex functions, such as those produced by image formation and shadow computation in 3D. Although automatic differentiation (AD) can generate these gradients, its inefficiency in higher dimensions makes it impractical for large-scale applications. This research presents an innovative, ad-hoc approach to accelerating the calculation of Jacobians in shadow determination by factorizing shadow strength into its constituent parts, thereby reducing computational complexity from O(N) to O(log N), where N represents the number of light sources. This new method, called factorized shadow differentiation (FSD), not only improves the efficiency of derivative calculations but also preserves mathematical accuracy. Our experiments have demonstrated the feasibility of this approach in real-time applications, such as optimizing complex functions and reconstructing objects from shadows, by providing results four times faster than AD without any loss in precision.

Recent studies in transportation networks have shown an increasing interest in uncertainty-aware path choice models. However, origin-destination (OD) demand is typically estimated as a fixed value and does not consider uncertainty in transportation networks. This paper addresses the estimation of a probability distribution for OD demand in an uncertain transportation network with daily route choice data available. OD demand is modeled with a Probabilistic Gaussian Process (PGP) distribution, maximizing its probability density function under constraints ensuring user equilibrium and transport conservation, resulting in an optimization problem with numerous variables and constraints. Since the optimization problem has a complex and non-differentiable objective, it is solved using an alternative algorithm based on penalization, leading to the recovery of statistical OD demand and travel time on links, followed by verification of the uniqueness of the solution. This unique solution is then used to develop an heuristics method to obtain the maximum likelihood estimate of the PGP parameters, leading to the development of an alternative optimization algorithm to achieve this goal using daily observed traffic data, resulting in the recovery of the OD demand probability distribution and the statistical variability of the transport times on the network's links.

In an array of nonlinear oscillators with random frequencies and purely conserved interactions, global phase coherence is demonstrated to occur within finite networks and further examined as it collapses through the generation of localized periodic and chaotic waves following a parameter adjustment. For weak nonlinearity in the system, these global phases exhibit a temporary state of order, resulting in the formation of coherent waves and phase defects. The phase defects' motion and interactions are then defined, where they are found to move in an anti-phase manner with the local energy oscillations. The obtained findings are applicable to multiple physical scenarios and offer a pathway to the creation of wave patterns through the manipulation of out-of-phase oscillations.

The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy in a single process. Ando et al. previously demonstrated that Wilson's algorithm can be modified to integrate Aldous-Broder for enhanced tree construction, and this integration appears to be exclusively beneficial. However, our findings challenge this view, showing that the integration can also generate uniform spanning trees in a different manner, and propose a two-step algorithm for tree construction where Wilson and Aldous-Broder are sequentially applied.

This work presents a comprehensive, annotated dataset called MusicTM-Dataset that comprises sheet music, lyrics, and musical audio. Our approach involves processing raw data using a pipeline to generate sheet music and lyrics representations, enabling feature alignment across different modalities. The resulting dataset offers three unique representation forms, facilitating sheet music, lyrics, and audio integration. This research aims to bridge the gap existing in music information retrieval by providing sheet music representation, unlike existing datasets that focus on audio-based representation only. The MusicTM-Dataset supports research in multimodal representation learning between sheet music, lyrics, and musical audio, promoting developments in tasks such as sheet music-based music information retrieval, sheet music-dependent genre classification, and audio-lyric alignment. The dataset and documentation are freely accessible at https://github.com/aiub-cs/MusicTM-Dataset.

One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in developing intuitive and user-friendly interfaces accessible to individuals who aren't technologically inclined. To address this, Ontodia enables diagrammatic data visualization, illustrated in our paper through examples from Wikidata. We've discovered that natural language processing and word vector techniques can enhance the exploration interface's capabilities, exemplified by our research demonstrating how such techniques facilitate the visualization and navigation of Visual Data Exploration with Ontodia and Wikidata.

The stability of dark solitons in one-dimensional systems that contain optical waveguides which adjust their refractive index based on intensity is examined within a two-component Gross-Pitaevskii framework. This study extends previous single-component research by incorporating systems composed of multiple coupled waveguides that exhibit varying dispersion characteristics. The analyzed black soliton corresponds to a stationary, oscillating solution that fully localizes in the bright component and is fully stable when there's matching dispersion for both components. When there's dispersion mismatch, however, the soliton becomes only partially stable, leading to a robust side mode instability where the dark soliton transforms into a grating of light spots. This phenomenon is further investigated by looking at how an impurity interacts with the soliton, specifically its ability to trap the impurity in cases of dispersion mismatch.

This research explores the concept of providing contextual assistance in visual analytics to help users make informed decisions, building on foundational work but aiming to introduce an approach suitable for practical applications. We present 'Lotse', a system designed to offer contextual clues, and illustrate its efficacy through the development of 'Lotse Weather', a real-world weather exploration tool. Our study positions Lotse within the frameworks of guided visual analytics and active learning. As a foundational concept, Lotse can support the creation of a wide range of applications, particularly those involving visual representations and interactive human-computer interactions, by providing enhanced user guidance.

We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in stellarator design is crucial, particularly for novel concepts. Our method achieves flexibility by aligning the equilibrium equilibrium with the target equilibrium in various configurations rather than aligning the coil planes. This ensures that the magnet coils function properly across all configurations, regardless of their strength. An illustrative example of this versatility is a set of seven designs spanning different beta values and rotation rates. Additionally, we discuss how our approach can be adapted for use with other types of stellarators.

Temperature variations within the interior of cylindrical fixed beds of 4-6 mm diameter, in both solid-solid and solid-solid-in-fluid configurations, were investigated using an advanced 3T MRI technique. This method enabled the direct mapping of temperature within the gas-solid systems. Prior to this, temperature distributions had been measured in solid-solid systems, but the application of the same method to gas-solid systems is a novel development. The mapping method's precision was verified through experiments where the temperature distribution of a step-function was measured in the vertical direction. Using this method, the longitudinal temperature profile was determined for the flow through a cylindrical fixed bed. Additionally, the transverse temperature profile was captured in the direction perpendicular to the flow's mean axis. These experiments demonstrated the feasibility of the MRI method for monitoring temperature variations in the interior of the fixed bed.

Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids spontaneously form membraneless droplets, referred to as biomolecular condensates, through a process of phase separation, thereby enabling biochemical reactions. Although it has been established that cells host numerous such condensates, the interactions between different components and their effects on phase separation have not been comprehensively understood. We have created a framework, leveraging the PyMSEF algorithm, to investigate the behavior of a mixture of multicomponent species exhibiting varying interactions. The model takes into account the presence of both self-assembly inducing and self-assembly inhibiting components within each species. By applying this framework to our analysis, we have found that the presence of different components within each species has an impact on condensate formation. Our results indicate that the specific interactions and compositions of these components can lead to both the promotion and inhibition of phase separation. The outcomes of our study also reveal that the size and number of droplets formed are influenced by both intra- and inter-species interactions and that the capacity for multiple condensates to co-exist in a cell is largely dependent on the specific interactions and compositions of their respective components.

Using the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we studied how a major leading sunspot rotated in NOAA AR 11429 during two powerful solar flares. A notable sunspot rotated in an unconventional direction, influenced significantly by the solar flares in October 2014. The evolution of the sunspots was divided into three distinct stages corresponding to the pre-, inter-, and post-flare periods. A sunspot moved slowly in a northward direction, accelerating its movement to the west just before an M6.7 class flare, which reached its peak speed one day later, causing an M5.1 class flare. Following this inter-flare period, the sunspots moved in an eastward direction, causing the sunspot 11429-C1 to appear in a new sunspot appearing near its original position. Outside of the sunspot complex, another sunspot emerged and moved in a southward direction, indicating deviation from typical differential rotation. Our research highlights the significant impact of solar flares on the movement and distribution of sunspots, displaying both accelerated and averted deviations from expected rotation patterns.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is directly implied by the principle.

This research involves comparing the multilevel preconditioning methods in cardiac mechanics, where the simulation models the interaction between the electrical signals and mechanical movements of the heart. These simulations are computationally intensive. To resolve this efficiently, we employ the finite element method combined with the finite difference method and the augmented Lagrange multiplier approach. Due to the complexity of these simulations, we apply multilevel preconditioners method consisting of algebraic multilevel preconditioner (AMG) for the matrix related to the mechanical movements and the Schur complement method using domain decomposition for the matrix associated with the electrical signals. These methods are scaled for large systems. The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of systems that support content creation, sharing, and management. Among these systems are tag-based platforms that enable users to collaborate in annotating shared items such as images and URLs, leading to user-generated metadata pools and collaborative behavior. To unlock users' potential, it is crucial to identify the characteristics of collaborative systems. This paper explores emerging systems for user content creation, and based on an original framework, presents an analysis of user-generated content and its associated tags, and reveals users' temporal behavior and collaboration patterns. Ultimately, this study proposes a model of collaborative system, and recommends design features to create effective collaborative systems.

Recently, proposed binary metagratings have the potential to revolutionize acoustic technology by enabling compact systems that can be integrated into small spaces. To achieve high performance, these microacoustic devices must operate at high frequencies, specifically above 1 MHz. This research presents a novel microacoustic metagrating design featuring a high-frequency resonator integrated into a DNA-patterning fabricated silica microchip. Through the use of two-photon lithography, precise metagrating structures were created on the resonator's surface, enabling the study and analysis of their acoustic behavior. The resulting experiments and simulations reveal the capability of the metagrating to effectively transmit and manipulate high-frequency acoustic waves.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of strong solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model. Utilizing the Fourier transform in space and carefully estimated inequalities, we demonstrate that the solutions converge to the global strong solution as time goes on. Moreover, by applying precise bounds on the solutions' weights in the Fourier domain, we obtain the convergence rate in the $L^2$-norm with respect to time.

Implementing integrated access and backhaul (IAB) in cellular networks via wireless links is a promising approach to streamline backhaul implementation, especially in densely deployed small cell networks. However, mobile IAB presents additional complexities due to the combination of mobility and wireless backhaul. A new framework for addressing the challenges of mobile IAB has been proposed in this work and its unique requirements and constraints will significantly expand the IAB paradigm. This paper delves into the complexities of mobile IAB and how it affects user connectivity and network reliability. To meet these needs, we review relevant wireles backhaul and mobility management technologies and discuss how they can address mobile IAB's challenges. Additionally, we highlight the outstanding research questions that need to be answered to successfully deploy mobile IAB.

This study employs two mainstream methods, Sobol and EFAST, of global sensitivity analysis to investigate the impact of key parameters in evolutionary algorithms on their ranking effectiveness. The investigation utilizes two standard performance metrics, spacing and extrapolation, of global sensitivity analysis to evaluate algorithmic hyperparameters. The results reveal that certain variables significantly influence the target function's output, whereas others have minimal effects. Based on these findings, we propose a simplified configuration of evolutionary algorithms that simplifies the process of determining suitable configurations. These recommendations are validated using two empirical test functions. The study's limitations are discussed, and potential areas for further research are identified.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when dealing with problems that extend beyond a single, confined setting.  Developing novel strategies to enable seamless adaptation in continuously evolving environments, known as continuous lifelong learning, is an intricate and complex task, with numerous potential issues stemming from restricted training data, memory limitations, and novel problem complexities.  To expedite research within this domain, we introduce L2Explorer, a new benchmark for reassessing reinforcement learning methods in extended, continuous environments.  This tool integrates modified versions of well-known retraining methods, combined with customized evaluation protocols, facilitating an in-depth analysis of their effectiveness across a range of benchmark scenarios.  The-L2Explorer package is readily available for download.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, features a customized data processing system developed in collaboration with the Keck Observatory. This system, designed to manage data from Liger observations, integrates data reduction tools and data management functionalities, ensuring seamless data flow between Liger and the Keck Observatory's data processing system. The data reduction system utilizes a customized data format for archival and analysis purposes, ensuring data integrity and efficiency. The system, written in C++, leverages existing software libraries and is designed to be easily integrated with other data processing tools and platforms.

This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial and smooth traveling wave patterns in 2D Euler equation solutions, existing in close proximity to the Couette flow. Our analysis shows that in 2D periodic domains, only a very limited set of traveling waves align with the Couette flow direction, implying an extensive variety of traveling waves with varying velocities and vorticity configurations. Notably, in contrast to 3D cases, our findings reveal the presence of traveling waves that exhibit non-zero reynolds stresses, implying a potential capacity to generate turbulence.

We experimentally control the linear polarization of exciton-polariton condensates using optical traps with elliptical geometries that favor specific polarization modes. Due to anisotropic splitting in the cavity, ground state degeneracy is lifted, yielding fine structure modes along the trap's axis and orthogonal to it. These modes are selectively occupied by the condensate. Our results reveal a unique method for polarization control with potential applications in spin-based photonics and research on complex optical systems with adjustable coupling properties.

This study's primary objective is to provide evidence and disproof for the deterministic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type equations including non-local gradient elements. The specific focus lies within a particular class of non-local terms. The investigation centers on determining if the given expressions can yield a well-defined, single-valued equation. For this purpose, we draw from an existing mathematical framework for non-local problems. Additionally, we leverage a previously established existence and uniqueness result from our own prior work.

The 2020 novel coronavirus outbreak in the world, including South Africa, led to the implementation of strict containment measures aimed at curbing its spread. Understanding the local epidemiology of the virus is essential for effective disease control and planning of healthcare systems. Following the identification of the first COVID-19 case in the Western Cape province in South Africa, health officials received an enormous number of potential cases through their hotlines daily. With limited financial resources and no existing surveillance systems to detect and monitor these cases, the provincial department of health initiated contact tracing through data provided by health care providers. This involves the submission of the patients' phone numbers to schedule follow-up appointments. However, the reliance on phone numbers raises concerns regarding data quality. The purpose of this paper is to examine the impact of incomplete data on contact tracing, as well as to explore how monitoring potential COVID-19 cases through phone numbers can provide valuable insights into the COVID-19 transmission dynamics in the Western Cape province. The study highlights how phone number-based monitoring enables the detection of high-risk individuals and facilitates the identification of potential outbreaks.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible sumsets from the sum of subsets A and B, where we show that under these constraints, A and B resemble arithmetic progressions more closely, with the degree of similarity tied to δ and ε. This result enhances previous findings and future implications stem from this improvement, allowing us to relate the lengths of subsets A and B more closely, where we use the notation [x] to mean the greatest integer less than or equal to x, and define the function h(δ) as the sum of 1 divided by δ and 3, plus an arbitrarily small positive real number ζ.

In the field of ophthalmology, diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma stand out as the two most prevalent conditions. Diabetic retinopathy is a complication arising from diabetes, while glaucoma is characterized by the erosion of optic disc cells. If left untreated, both conditions can lead to vision impairment and blindness. A prominent method for diagnosing these conditions involves analyzing the fundus images of the retina. Our research introduces a novel deep learning method that utilizes information from multiple sources to accurately classify grained images of the retina. This approach starts by using transfer learning to extract features from the fundus images, which are then split into the upper and lower portions. Each portion is then processed through separate 2D-CNNs to ultimately produce class probabilities. By fusing the output from the two branches, the model achieves accurate classification of the retina images. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, with the following performance records: 97% accuracy in identifying glaucoma using AIOSI-Net, 98% using C-ResNet50, and 99% using C-ResNet101; similarly, in the field of diabetic retinopathy, the method achieved performance records of 98%, 99%, and 100% accuracy using the same models, respectively.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics that can help predict the need for ICU treatment in COVID-19 patients. Researchers aimed to identify how COVID-19 severity in X-ray images is expressed. To this end, they assembled a database of 8,000 annotated X-ray images, investigating the disease's spread patterns, affected severity levels, and radiological features. Additionally, they identified and studied the relationship between clinical symptoms and radiological signs. Using these findings, they created a dataset, USD-CT, to train a deep learning model, which was used to analyze the need for ICU treatment based on whether patients had COVID-19 symptoms listed in their clinical records.
