The results showed that the model achieved 69% accuracy in predicting ICU treatment requirements, with certain clinical symptoms being better predictors than others.

We analyze the transmission eigenvalue problem for the Helmholtz equation, focusing on the case where the refractive index varies in a spherical and layered manner, leading to a second-order ODE known as the Li\'enard equation, with boundary conditions that diminish at infinity. We prove that the transmission eigenfunctions, associated with this system, are uniquely localized at either the inner or outer boundary, depending on the eigenvalue parameter. Our findings are validated through numerical simulations, which also examine the impact of different boundary conditions on transmission eigenvalues and identify potential exceptions to our main conclusion. This study offers a theoretical foundation for time-reversal focused ultrasound imaging, as it shows that time-reversed transmission eigenfunctions yield precise spatial samples at specific boundaries, which are more physically relevant than the overall transmission eigenvalues.

To expand a dialogue system's capabilities, discovering new intent categories from user inputs is essential for real-world applications. While existing methods rely on manually labeled data, they are impractical due to their labor-intensive requirements, and unsupervised methods, though eliminating labeling costs, suffer from low performance due to lack of guidance. We propose a novel approach that combines pre-training and contrastive learning to discover new intent categories without labels, and significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks for intent discovery.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.
In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ possesses no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ subgroups.

This study re-examines the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation. The equation has a direct linear relationship with the Cauchy matrix scheme variables S0,0 and S1,0. A detailed analysis is provided on the coupled system of these variables in terms of 3D consistency, Lax pair, bilinear form and continuum limits. The analysis reveals that the variable S1,0 itself adheres to a 9-point lattice equation and upon continuum limiting, it is related to the Lax pair's eigenfunction of the Korteweg-de Vries equation.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discover that the spatial relationship between objects is often overlaid with irrelevant background elements, leading the model to mistakenly identify valid relationships between the objects and the background in VRD. Consequently, we propose Two-Stage Visual Relationship Detection (TSVRD), a straightforward yet effective framework that overcomes this challenge in standard VRD. TSVRD is composed of two distinct stages: tVRD and sVRD. In the initial stage, tVRD enhances the focus on the objects and their surroundings by employing a multi-scale non-parallel feature extraction and a deformable grid pooling, thereby capturing fine-grained object characteristics and their context more effectively than standard VRD. Subsequently, the refined feature map is integrated with standard VRD networks to form sVRD, a adaptive re-detection module that further refines the model's ability to distinguish between relevant and irrelevant context, an capability that is critically important for addressing the issue of false positives in VRD. Experimental results confirm that both stage tVRD and sVRD significantly outperform standard VRD models, effectively mitigating the issue of false positives in VRD. Code will be made available online at https://github.com/Cheng-Wei-Lin/TSVRD.

A new measure, quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing Bell-state measurement (BSM). It's demonstrated that the QCC is not solely dependent on the degree of entanglement but also on the state's orientation in the entanglement dimension. Furthermore, experiments have shown that using superconducting qubits, we can achieve entanglement with low QCC by employing a specific strategy.

Artificial intelligence systems that simulate human social interactions are critical in creating believable virtual agents. A significant challenge lies in automatically modeling social relationships among agents, given that these connections are usually represented as diverse, disconnected graphs. In this study, we focus on developing an AI model that uses text-based social relationships to produce a graph that captures the social connections, with its nodes representing individual agents and its edges denoting their interactions. To overcome the difficulty of modeling social relationships, which involve variable node and edge counts, we introduce an advanced neural network called the Social Relationship Graph Generation (SRGG) model. The SRGG model produces graphs that more closely resemble the input text and outperforms existing methods in preserving the structure of given social relationship graphs.

Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is crucial for achieving a comprehensive comprehension of images. Convolutional neural networks are effective at capturing local patterns but often struggle with global understanding. Transformers are capable of modeling long-range relationships; however, their computational complexity grows quadratically with input size, making them impractical for large-scale image processing. In contrast to Transformers and CNNs, we propose a new approach called message passing networks (MPNs) that can efficiently process scenes of any size. Our dynamic graph MPMs introduce a graph-based message passing mechanism that outperforms existing CNN and Transformer methods on long-shot COCO instances, while providing comparable performance on short-shot scenarios.

Optimizing hardware efficiency in digital systems, specifically through the Multiple Constant Multiplication problem, has long been a significant challenge.  Successful resolution of this optimization allows a single multiplier to execute various constant multiplications swiftly, enhancing the performance of diverse applications like digital filters, complex multiplication, and polynomial evaluations.  This work presents an innovative and efficient approach to tackle the MCC problem, distinguishing itself from existing solutions due to its unique capabilities of scaling to any input size and supporting both fixed and variable inputs.  The proposed algorithm's core is an advanced graph-based technique that redefines the traditional hardware costs for multipliers with multiple constants.  By integrating a new resource: shared 'or-tree' structures, the method achieves a substantial reduction in total multi-operand adder costs, leading to a net decrease of 25% to 60% compared to the best-known solutions.  The efficacy of this approach is showcased through exemplary methods for processing 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 input constants, along with a strategy for scaling to larger input sizes using a novel tree architecture.  Moreover, this method can be adapted to handle variable inputs at no additional expense, yielding impressive performance gains of up to 37.5% less hardware cost over the current best solutions.

Quantum machine learning has emerged as a cutting-edge area within quantum computing, aiming to harness the power of quantum algorithms and circuits for enhanced machine learning tasks. Among various approaches, Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) stand out as a prominent method. Recently, significant advancements have been made in QNNs. Unfortunately, these advancements are not widely known among practitioners, largely due to the lack of comprehensive surveys that can help bridge this knowledge gap. In response to this need, we present this survey, which thoroughly introduces the fundamentals of QNNs along with their underlying quantum algorithms and circuits. Additionally, we discuss current challenges in QNNs. Our aim is for this survey to serve as a valuable resource for both beginners and practitioners of quantum machine learning.

The radio frequency (RF) accelerator technology forms the backbone of nearly all modern particle and nuclear physics experiments, as well as applications in chemistry, biology, and medical imaging. This year, the RF accelerator community plans to undertake an in-depth analysis of the status and prospects of conventional and innovative RF accelerator technologies, subsequently presenting the findings to the broader Snowmass community.

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. The former models exhibit rotation for certain types of fluid waves and this rotation is linked to viscosity. Furthermore, the two models converge in the long-wavelength limit. To better understand the framework of the primary approximation, we developed a resummation method that yields accurate results for a broader range of spatial wavelengths.

Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. We have found that the strength of this emission is heavily reliant on the mass of the black hole, its impact parameter relative to the wavelength of the radiation, and the spin of the particle being emitted. In the case of black holes with a mass less than the square of the Planck mass, the analysis is complicated due to the formation of an effective horizon within the quantum tunneling process. To address this complexity, we have introduced the concept of quantum apparent horizons. By using quantum apparent horizons, we have shown that the traditional black hole background emission rates remain applicable. However, the total emission rate is directly related to the probability of the black hole actually containing a singularity. Assuming the distribution function of primordial black holes follows the Bell-Szekeres model, we have calculated the specific emission rates of radio waves, and the results indicate that the PBH background radiation is unlikely to be the cause of the observed anomalies.

Introducing the Virtual Secure Platform (VSP), a pioneering solution that brings together multi-party computation (MPC) and public cryptography to secure entire computing systems. VSP is built on top of the TinyFPHE (TFHE) scheme, an emerging method for efficient cryptographic operations on binary matrices. This makes VSP the first secure platform available in a cloud environment, offering a secure environment for code execution and data access. This paper introduces the VSP as a binary multiplier-five-stage pipeline processor, designed to verify its performance, measure its efficiency, and showcase its potential advantages. VSP's high robustness is demonstrated by its ability to tolerate errors, while its low overhead is reflected in its minimal latency increase of 5.12 times and 10.24 times over secret and public inputs, respectively. Compared to traditional computing systems, VSP's primary challenge is utilizing an public interface, resulting in a 0.00005 to 0.00006 seconds increase in execution time.

We developed an efficient, polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for a broad category of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), specifically those that can be defined over arbitrary finite constraints but have the property of being solvable with few constraints per variable in the sparse formulation. Our PTAS outperforms the best previously known results, achieving an approximation factor of $O(n^4)$ compared to $O(n^6)$. Furthermore, we found that achieving certain logarithmic approximation ratios, such as $O(\log n)$, presents a challenge only under the assumption that NP is difficult to solve polynomially.

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactic information, as demonstrated in previous studies. This work presents models that leverage pre-trained language models for part-of-speech tagging and dependency parsing, either alone or in combination with a small amount of annotated data. When used unsupervised, these models achieve state-of-the-art results on the datasets of WallStreet News and WikiText-2. Moreover, they demonstrate exceptional few-shot performance, outperforming models trained exclusively with annotated data on the WallStreet World-2 dataset, and matching the accuracy of models trained with full supervision on the CHST dataset.

High-resolution hyperspectral images possess the unique capability of capturing detailed spectral information across various frequencies, albeit with lower resolution compared to ordinary RGB images. The enormous amount of data in these images, specifically the spectral bands, has led to their exploration in innovative applications, such as employing machine learning methods for cityscape semantic segmentation in hyperspectral images. The presence of substantial spectral data enables a novel approach to cityscape object classification and segmentation, even with limited labels. The enormous amount of spectral information in these images has led to the development of new techniques for segmentation, even with limited labels. The huge spectral data in these images has led to exploration of innovative methods for cityscape object classification and segmentation. The presence of detailed spectral information in these images has led to the exploration of novel methods for hyperspectral image segmentation. The enormous amount of data in these images, specifically the spectral bands, has led to the investigation of applying machine learning methods for hyperspectral image segmentation. The huge spectral data in these images, specifically the spectral bands, has led to the investigation of using machine learning methods for hyperspectral image segmentation.

This study reveals that a specific star, HD 156869, possesses characteristics of an old, slowly rotating solar-type star, yet exhibits a substantial amount of disk material. Typically, similar stars should have fully dispersed any initial protostellar disks by now, and are expected to rotate much slower. Researchers hypothesize two main possibilities for this anomaly - either the star engaged in a unique interaction with a nearby planet, or it developed exceptional angular momentum retention capabilities. A detailed analysis of the star's photoevaporation and rotation dynamics suggests an interaction with a planet is the most plausible explanation, specifically one that didn't follow standard tidal expectations. This study emphasizes the importance of carefully evaluating astrophysical anomalies to refine our understanding of planet and star formation processes.

In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being the standard for analysis, the RAM model has received surprisingly little attention from theoretical researchers compared to other computation models. This paper aims to investigate the efficiency of basic arithmetic operations within the RAM model, where the cost of each computation is determined by the number of instructions rather than the size of their data. We focus specifically on operations that can be performed in constant time and are closed under composition. Our key findings include the demonstration that the exponential function cannot be computed in constant time with a basic set of instructions, while several other arithmetic operations can be computed with basic programs; and we establish a framework allowing for efficient computation of functions based on the properties of Turing closure under a broader set of RAM operations.

To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting session-based recommendation models that predict the next item users will choose, researchers combined self-supervised learning with co-training. They proposed an enhanced framework by leveraging a session-based graph to create informative, not artificially sparse, data for these models. This new approach exploits internal and external session connections to produce contrastive learning, thereby preserving genuine session data for superior session-based recommendation performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the success of this innovative method in achieving state-of-the-art results on session-based recommendation tasks.

This research presents a method for creating weak group reversible LCD codes of any length and block size using the group algebra approach, which can then be upgraded to standard group reversible LCD codes if specific conditions are satisfied. It also presents a method for generating group LCD codes that can be transformed into cyclic or reversible LCD codes via the ensemble method and a search technique, as well as a greedy algorithm for optimizing group LCD codes. The efficiency and practical applicability of the proposed methods are demonstrated through the construction of various group LCD and group reversible LCD codes.

We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the matroid and graph complex to it. It's suggested that these differential forms, potentially undefined in certain regions, can serve as regulated versions of Feynman integrals within the given compactification, offering a new method to compute and understand these integrals, particularly the double-spectra in multi-loop scattering amplitudes.

In an study on recurrent artificial neural networks, we found that when trained for specific object categorization tasks, the network's default processing path is redirected away from general features and towards category-specific information about the test input's object. This shift in focus is triggered by a unique signal derived from the test input, it also helps the network achieve higher accuracy in its current categorization task. Furthermore, we discovered that this shift persists even when the network's underlying dynamics are masked, suggesting that it is surrounded by non-object inputs. In contrast, when the test input belongs to a different category than the network's default training, we found that the category-specific signal has no impact on the network's processing of other input information.

Despite significant research on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations on topological properties has been largely unexplored. Our work investigates how correlations affect the topological characteristics of one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems with multiple bands. We demonstrate that in systems with multiple bands, correlations can reduce or even eliminate the topological phases that exist in single-body systems. This occurrence happens because the ground state of such systems exhibits interplay between different sectors, causing a shift in the effective Brillouin zone as a result of correlation effects. Our results indicate that the topological properties of such systems are inherently influenced by correlation effects and, consequently, the single-body assumption is insufficient to describe these properties accurately.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices of any size and the unitary polyphase matrices that represent them were introduced, which enable the generation of multi-phase complementary sequences via their rows. This build-up to Golay complementary phasarray (GCPA) structures allows us to develop GCPAs of multiple phases with high dimensions. This work develops a novel framework to develop polyphase GCPAs, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through the creation of 2-phase GCPAs with difference sets foundation and general constructions with the complement of rectangular GCPAs, as well as a method to merge the rows of GCPAs to form their column concatenations.

The nature of the Higgs boson is being explored and compared to the predictions of the Standard Model. Experimental off-shell and on-shell production rates of the Higgs boson are analyzed in four-lepton events. Data collected at a 13 TeV energy level by the ATLAS detector, comprising 36.1 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity of proton-proton collisions, were used to conduct these comparisons. Measured off-shell and on-shell production rates exhibit inconsistencies with the Standard Model predictions, allowing researchers to set a width upper limit of 4.1 GeV for the Higgs boson, which in turn suggests a 95% confidence level constraint of -28 to 10 GeV for its decay width. Also, anomalous couplings related to the Higgs boson and vector bosons are calculated and found to lie within a specific range, indicating deviations that could signify the presence of new physics beyond the Standard Model.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the complexities of analyzing numerous spectral bands within bi-temporal hyperspectral images. This study proposes a cutting-edge approach using a novel deep convolutional autoencoder that fuses features across hierarchical levels and receptive fields. By utilizing an unsupervised change detection technique, it overcomes the limitations of other label-dependent methods. By integrating various techniques to extract changes from the images, it significantly outperformed current state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised change detection across diverse datasets.

Consider the set $\mathcal{S}$, defined as all squares of natural numbers. We're examining the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ in relation to $\mathcal{S}$, specifically whether the sum of $\mathbb{N}$ with a given subset $A$ of $\mathcal{S}$ covers all natural numbers greater than some threshold $B$. We're providing an asymptotic estimate for the count of such $A$ and $B$ pairs, with the evaluation reliant on the work of Daif and one of the authors from earlier work.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that transcends conventional chemical and physical barriers in nature. Within atomic lattices, this phenomenon is heavily influenced by lattice symmetry, giving rise to path symmetries and associated interference patterns. This is particularly evident in the behavior of electrons and holes in silicon, where lattice interference affects both charge and spin properties, with direct implications for quantum computing and spintronic devices. Research has shown that lattice interference in silicon affects the phase relationship between orthogonal valley states, influencing the valley-locked spin orientation of tunneling events. Consequences of this phase relationship are observable in silicon tunnel junctions, where they give rise to spin-polarized current anomalies dependent on the orientation of the device structure. Furthermore, this phenomenon is also seen in chemically terminated silicon quantum point contacts, where interference patterns can be manipulated by altering the depth of the confinement state, thereby revealing a previously unexplored spin-polarized conductance behavior.

Optimal control is a well-established field with applications in various industries, but making it accessible to engineers without specialized mathematics expertise has been challenging. To address this, we introduce a novel, intuitive, and open-source tool, LibOPT, that streamlines the development and deployment of optimization algorithms with minimal effort. This open-source platform allows for the rapid creation of complex models utilizing a variety of optimization techniques and facilitates their deployment on a wide array of hardware, including workstations and embedded systems, as well as through various programming interfaces. Our aim with LibOPT is to make optimal control more approachable and intuitive, facilitating the evolution of new techniques and their practical application in real-world scenarios. This open-source project embraces collaboration and community-driven development to continue expanding its capabilities.

Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is defined as the largest integer m such that Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X, allowing us to classify the variety based on this transitivity degree and the properties of Aut(X) being either primitive or imprimitive. If the degree of transitivity is at least m plus one and Aut(X) exhibits primitive characteristics, then there exists a group of automorphisms G that is either almost simple or simple, and similar in structure to it, whose action on X is nearly simple, with the exception of cases where G and its normal core in Aut(X) only differ by a finite group, except for a small number of identified exceptions. In cases with non-simple action, additional constraints apply which can be listed.

In non-commutative space-time deformations, the definition of identical particles breaks down. These models are described by non-abelian space symmetries represented by a four-momentum group. Our approach recognizes that for multi-particle states, the total system momentum is the only well-defined property. Calculating the total momentum involves non-commutative composition rules. Our results indicate that non-commutative space-time, defined by a constant tensor, leads to observable effects at two-body interaction levels. We demonstrate this with the scattering of two quantum particles and the quantization of non-commutative rigid bodies.

We have employed the two-photon absorption edge transient current technique to investigate the charge transport properties in high-quality synthetic single-crystalline diamond. The 2PHOTETS technique involves using two-photon excitation to generate carriers and has shown immense potential in characterizing charge transport within wide-bandgap materials. Our experiments involved 1030 nm pulsed laser excitation, which triggered two-photon absorption in the diamond's wide bandgap, and this was followed by measuring the edge transient current in the diamond. This current was modeled theoretically, demonstrating that 2PHOTETS enables independent measurement of horizontal and vertical charge movement. Based on these measurements, we were able to determine the mobility of holes and electrons, finding their mobility to be 446 cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ and 1811 cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$, respectively. The electron transport appears relatively more efficient, likely due to the use of grown-in diamonds with superior quality and lower impurity levels. The technique's ability to investigate synthetic single-crystalline diamond's charge transport opens up possibilities for its application in advanced diamond electronics, sensors, and other cutting-edge diamond-based technologies.

Social media platforms are facing significant issues with hate speech propagation, which demands the development of advanced NLP techniques to identify and categorize such content. This research presents a comprehensive analysis of the performance of modern transformer-based language models in tackling the problems of identifying and classifying hate speech on Arabic social media, specifically focused on misogyny. The findings indicate that combining multiple deep learning models can enhance accuracy, and a new framework built on this concept achieved exceptional results in the first misogyny identification and classification competition on Arabic social media. The model's source code and trained weights are freely available on GitHub.

This study centres around the solvability of a distinct class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations that take into account past influences within their generators, under Lipschitz condition it's demonstrated that the existence and uniqueness of such equations are assured. Furthermore, a key comparison theorem has been formulated.

We examine if models trained for control purposes can be used to develop controllers that function reliably in situations with uncertain conditions. A controller is considered robust if it provides the same level of performance across different scenarios. We introduce an approach that leverages a environment model to optimize the robustness of controllers in different situations. This involves building a stochastic control model that incorporates uncertainty in its structure. We then develop an algorithm to efficiently explore the control actions available to improve robustness, using the information provided by the environment model. This approach was tested on two types of problems: continuous-time dynamics control and grid-world tasks with varying dynamics. Results indicate that the proposed method outperforms other techniques and is capable of discovering robust controllers in situations where other methods fail.

Several key networks and systems such as caching, database retrieval, and distributed computation face efficiency and latency issues during peak times due to excessive backhaul traffic. A general approach has been developed that encompasses both caching and distributed computation techniques, allowing insights in one area to benefit the other. Our framework builds upon previously established methods, including coded caching and computation, and makes the following contributions: ((i) The unified framework integrates previous research, (ii) The results of our approach exceed those of previous studies by( $(1-FX)/F+1$) times in optimal external network demand, (iii) With $F$ subfiles and $X$ files held by users, ( $(1-X/F)$) times improved performance achieved in computation scheme with uncached inputs and exact matching results seen in caching scheme with cached inputs; (iv) With $X$ files and $F$ subsets, subsets' requests can be fully served at $\frac{1-F(1-X/F)}{F}$ external network demand when $I;X/F;1$; and computation scheme with fully cached inputs sees inputs at $\frac{1-F(1-X/F)}{F}$ times external network demand

We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, employing it to prove an existence theorem for PCF semantics. Our model relies on the property of univalence to confirm that our definition satisfies the necessary congruence requirements. The proof is carried out without invoking the axiom of choice, making it a direct consequence of univalent type theory. Additionally, we observe that on sets, our Scott model coincides with the standard domain-theoretic Scott model, and even when the choice axiom is available, our model is provably equivalent to the Scott model based on Tarski's definition in univalent type theory.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity.

Quantum information can be manipulated in Bose-Einstein condensates through the application of Konig's nonlinear gate concept. This involves employing two kernels: a duplication gate that creates two copies of the condensate, and a controlled-NOT gate that flips one copy in response to an input signal, ultimately yielding two condensates embodying the original input and control information. Our research focuses on realizing these operations using the interaction of a single control beam with two distinct traps.

This paper aims to accomplish two distinct objectives. Firstly, it seeks to establish a unicity theorem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, under the constraint of limited intersection with hypersurfaces. Secondly, the paper aims to prove a unicity theorem for the case of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share a specified number of hyperplanes in a particular geometric configuration.

Polynomial systems with non-degenerate solutions play a crucial role in multiple disciplines. We've developed a new algorithm to compute the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system, defined as the set of points that satisfy the Jacobian determinant equal to zero along with the original system's equations. This algorithm leverages breakthrough results from location theory, employing signature-based methods to efficiently count real solutions. We implemented our algorithm using BSDMathE's signature verification tools, obtaining exact counts of real connected components for counter-example systems and providing real solution counts for example systems of fixed degree.

Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^+$+$e^-$ combined yield relative to hadrons, we found that photon production exceeds expectations based on nucleon $p$-$p$ collisions at lower energies by a significant margin, especially at $2\%$ centrality where it is over ten times higher. This is consistent with hydrodynamic models that show the effect of cumulative minijet effects over the entire photon path, resulting in increased production. In contrast, semi-hard minijet models overestimate photon production and are excluded. Photons were found to exceed thermal field theory estimates at both midrapidity and for more peripheral events. Estimates of nucleon $p$-$p$ collisions at 388 GeV were made.

The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotically optimal upper bound for the squared l2-norm of K4^3-free tripartite hypergraphs' degree vectors. This work provides novel upper bounds on the Turan density of the tetrahedron, which in turn, yields improved upper bounds for the l1 and l2 norms for the tripartite case. Additionally, we derive exact results for the l1-norm of non-tetrahedron 3-uniform hypergraphs and the tripartite case, which specifically gives the score for the Levenshtein (1971) and Nikiforov's (2017) constructions. Furthermore, we determine asymptotically optimal upper bounds for the tripartite score of the l1 and l2-norms for the induced tripartite K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraphs.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating anti-aliased line joins through the combination of triangle fills and rasterization, resulting in performance issues. In an effort to address these limitations, a novel technique has been developed that leverages the rendering capabilities of OpenGL API to produce anti-aliased line joins while avoiding the direct approximation of triangle vertices. This results in improved visual quality, enhanced user experience, and optimized performance. A comparative analysis confirms the efficacy of the proposed method, rendering maps with line joins 2 times faster than the alternative approximation approach, and 1.5 times faster than utilizing the standard OpenGL API.

The multivariate interpolation problem is often challenging due to its complexity. This work presents a novel RBF with transcendental properties that overcomes limitations of existing SCBFs, ensuring continuity and $C^\infty$ smoothness for any parameter choice. The studied RBF possesses unique properties, being both positive and conditionally strictly non-negative, and is stable in all relevant function spaces. The paper also delves into the SCBF's behavior in relation to existing RBFs and presents a novel, shape-preserving quasi-interpolation operator that yields bounds on the infinite matrix norm. The convergence of this operator is also examined.

Pulsar wind nebulas within galaxy wind nebulae are dynamic systems driven by the interaction between pulsar radiation and magnetohydrodynamic winds, generating X-rays and gamma-rays that are detectable by space and ground-based telescopes. These gamma-rays are also scattered into higher-energy gamma-ray pulsar halos by the wind particles. Observations from telescopes like the Cherenkov Telescope Array and the Integral Field Unit Telescope have unveiled gamma-ray pulsar halos at distances of up to 3.5 kiloparsecs, revealing intricate patterns of particle interactions and shedding light on the physics governing these cosmic phenomena. These discoveries have significant implications for understanding the life cycles of neutron stars and their role in shaping galaxy evolution.

Classifying weather scenes is crucial in various fields such as agriculture, energy, and transportation. Recent advancements in deep learning have shown exceptional performance in this task. However, this problem has received less attention, and previous works lack thorough evaluations. We present the Weather Classification dataset, along with significant findings on convolutional neural networks. This dataset comprises multi-category weather scenes, accompanied by detailed annotations. Our research explores the efficacy of several data augmentation techniques and the [Dropout](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2016.11.026v1) regularization method. Furthermore, we compare multiple architectures, testing them on our dataset and reporting comprehensive results, including exact match performance and the [Hamming distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamming_distance).

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later.

Soft grippers, characterized by their low weight and flexibility, are ideal for robotic applications involving deformation and instability. However, their complexity poses challenges for inversion and tractability. This research introduces an online control system for a novel, lightweight soft multi-fingered gripper, utilizing the Koopman operator to translate non-linear dynamics into a linear framework. The initial model, based on the finite element method, enables precise simulation but lacks scalability. To address this, we develop a model order reduction technique and propose a trial-and-error online adjustment method to compensate for model inaccuracies and control performance degradation. The online adaptation can restore and maintain control performance.

One of the primary objectives in learning from data lies in optimizing statistical models. In line with this goal, a broad framework for counterfactual reasoning has been formulated. Within this framework, both Statistical Model Theoretic (SMT) and Causal Model Theoretic (CMT) approaches aim to discover optimal policies or treatments, yet they employ distinct proof techniques. This work showcases how concepts and results from CMT can be applied to SMT, effectively extending popular algorithms such as the Statistical Model Theoretic (SMT) algorithm and Causal Model Theoretic (CMT) algorithm. Notably, our study's findings support the development of the semi-Supervised Statistical Model Theoretic (SSSMT) and Causal Model Theoretic (CSMTM) algorithms. Moreover, our research informs the design of algorithms by offering guidance on selecting appropriate estimators. Crucially, our study's implications reveal a connection between these algorithms and the Natural Gradient Descent (NGD) principle, thereby guiding their future development.

High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look into the black hole activity in the early universe. Specifically, misaligned jets of high-energy particles are a common feature of young black holes. Researchers discovered a particularly distant young black hole source on April 24, 2021. This high-energy object is situated in a galaxy far away, approximately 4.95 billion years from us, and has a uniquely shaped jet pointing in a different direction than expected. Its brightness and orientation suggest that it is a sign of a young black hole, and its properties match those of similar objects. Interestingly, it is located near a more common type of galaxy that has been observed to have black holes at the same distance, but with different alignment. Further observations and studies will be needed to understand these galaxies and their high-energy objects, including how they formed and developed.

This research focuses on developing an efficient and reliable method for predicting survival outcomes in patients diagnosed with non-small cell lung cancer. Combining genetic and imaging information, individualized predictions are made. First, specific gene expressions are identified using nested cross-validation, and their association with survival is evaluated through metrics like concordance index, penalized regression, and feature selection. Next, radiomic features are extracted and selected, with features being fine-tuned based on their associations with the previously identified genetic profile. Finally, an image+gene model is created, and its performance is compared to the gene-only model. We evaluated our approach using data from the TCIA institute, involving 269 NSCLC patients, and found that the proposed method outperformed the gene-only model, with improved predictions of overall survival, particularly for specific patient subgroups, and identified the top contributing modality-specific features.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations from absorption spectra of quasas within a fixed range. Leveraging extensive simulations generated with the FALCON code, this method utilizes neural networks to analyze matter distribution on various scales. Our reconstruction algorithm exhibits high accuracy within the trained redshift range and exhibits diminishing error as redshift increases beyond the training set. Notably, even significant changes to the underlying simulation model have minimal impact on our results. Furthermore, we successfully apply our reconstruction technique to low-redshift optical baryonic acoustic oscillation data with high accuracy.

This paper examines certain types of non- free modules over Lie algebras of differential operators, specifically those related to functions on a $1$-dimensional manifold, and demonstrates their relationship with free modules over the universal envelope of the Lie algebra, $\mathfrak h$, also establishes which sections are free from the action of $U(\frak h)$.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue systems have significantly improved the overall quality of conversational agents. However, creating high-quality, diverse, and diverse conversational agents remains a major challenge, especially for systems designed to emulate the behavior of particular characters. Despite numerous efforts, open-domain dialogue systems with specific, defined roles are still relatively underdeveloped in both research and industry applications. This paper outlines a strategy for developing a role-based chatbot, powered by large-scale language models, comparable to human-level performance. Our system, designed to emulate conversations typical of a popular female personality, achieved remarkable results, with a Causal-permutational Metric of 1.26 and minimal deviation from human-written responses. Our findings suggest that this approach is a viable alternative to existing methods, with potential to transform open-domain dialogue systems by enabling finer control over system behavior and greater flexibility in developing systems that mimic human conversations.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory signal, whose characteristics differ from standard gravitational waves. Researchers have determined the properties of this memory signal and found that it can be detected by current detectors like LIGO and future detectors like Einstein Telescope within the 10-30 Hz range at its peak. Even the Event Horizon Telescope can potentially pick up signals below 10-30 Hz due to the vast spatial scales involved, and the detection of these events may offer new opportunities to study black hole populations and the universe.

A supersymmetry breaking phase transition within a hypercompact star provides the means for generating both gravity waves and left-right symmetry through the mechanism of left-right symmetric supersymmetric leptogenesis. The phase transition between two CPEs in the superpotential triggers the separation of the R-symmetry, resulting in the generation of gravity waves during the process. Furthermore, R-symmetry breaking leads to the appearance of a potential barrier within the Kretschmann scalar field, which in turn triggers the collapse of the star into a black hole. The superpotential and the Boltzmann equation are used to determine the amount of baryon asymmetry within the star, whereas Einstein's field equations are solved using numerical methods to examine the effects of the star's inhomogeneities on the geometry within the star. The study demonstrates consistency between gravity waves detected by LIGO and VIGO with the predicted outcomes from the leptogenesis mechanism within the superpotential, which also allows us to obtain Penrose diagrams inside the resulting black hole.

A reliable and efficient communication system that transcends traditional causes and effects is emerging in the form of semantic communications. An unexpected challenge is that messages in this cause-and-effect system do not always share the same meaning. To overcome this issue, researchers have been exploring signaling games to develop a communication method that naturally arises from the game. However, reaching a stable and meaningful cause-and-effect loop within a complex real-world environment remains difficult. To tackle this issue, a new neuro-symbolic approach to causal reasoning is employed, incorporating a model that infers a latent variable and generates a semantic message that maximizes the effects on the environment. This approach also includes a planning system that finds the most optimal and efficient message to transmit, and a signaling game that naturally induces a communication method that causes and effects within the environment. Through this approach, researchers have demonstrated that the collective agents reach a stable and efficient cause-and-effect loop within a complex real-world environment. A simulation on a traffic control system has shown that this approach can significantly improve the environmental effect by inducing a latent semantic message that causes and effects within the environment.

The Natural Language Processing (NLP) task of predicting the next word in a sentence is referred to as the word prediction (WP) problem. A significant approach to solving WP, known as the n-gram method, relies on using knowledge of word sequences. However, models based on n-gram methods often fail to effectively capture long-range word dependencies. Another set of methods, known as neural word prediction (NWP) models, uses continuous representations of words but can struggle to fully capture semantic relationships between multiple words. Recently, researchers have combined n-gram and neural methods to improve the accuracy of word prediction, but such models still struggle to accurately anticipate words located far from those being processed. Our proposed solution, a hybrid model, integrates the advantages of both n-gram and neural approaches, and also utilizes a word-bag representation to capture non-local semantic relationships. This new model, when evaluated on the standard benchmark of the WikiText-2 dataset, demonstrated improved accuracy, achieving a lower word error rate of 25.92%.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates and reasonable computation times and storage requirements. Typically, these systems focus on maximizing the precision of next item predictions while employing learned continuous vector representations, known as embed-dings, for item sequences. In this research, we propose integrating frequency rank encod-ing into the embedding learning process for a given sequence of items. By doing so, we aim to enhance the performance of session-based recommenders by leveraging both item similarity and their occurrence frequencies. Additionally, our approach offers a computationally efficient pre-ranking strategy to streamline the recommendation pipeline without derailing training convergence. Experimental evaluations on public datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method in terms of accuracy and its efficiency in terms of computation time.

We investigate a rigid arrangement of two active colloids held together by a ligand, specifically examining its dynamic behavior in activity gradients within a viscous environment lacking external influences. Research reveals that this molecular configuration exhibits active rotations around its axis, driven by disparities in activity levels affecting each constituent colloid. Furthermore, we establish that a distinct orientation emerges for molecules within these gradients, accompanied by unique orientation patterns when considering their distribution along the molecular axis. Additionally, we analyze how factors such as activity magnitude and asymmetry influence the molecular axis period and explain their variation based on a straightforward theoretical model.

A thorough investigation of three-dimensional discrete fracture network simulations is presented. We utilize the Mimetic Finite Difference method to develop a flexible and easily implementable simulator. A specific focus is given to the representation of fractures within a discrete fracture matrix model using the conforming discrete fracture network approach. We explain how to model non-conforming fracture geometries by creating an additional mesh specifically for fractures within the overall domain mesh. This involves splitting the overall mesh into separate fracture and matrix sub-meshes through a process known as mesh partitioning. We detail the techniques for mesh partitioning, as well as the methods for forming conforming cell interfaces and accurately representing fracture properties when there is a size difference between the fracture and domain meshes. We provide the corresponding code from our SFM3D simulator which can be accessed through our GitHub repository at https://github.com/ENSTA-paris/SFM3D.

This study showcases a novel application of drone technology in an outdoor educational setting, utilizing a swarm of drones to create and maintain three-dimensional cell structures with lights. The same framework serves as a collision avoidance and position-tracking system within the swarm. The authors rely on centroid-based registration algorithms to facilitate inter-dance communication and provide essential information for planning movements within and between the structures. The research describes how this approach supports multiple applications, including the creation of cellular formations, maintenance of these formations, and avoidance of collisions.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always part of its spectrum. We derive exact expressions for the Seidel spectrum and Secant energy, given that such a graph has $n$ vertices and its Seidel matrix possesses two distinct eigenvalues.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking the set of elliptic potentials to the set of periodic potentials.

RSUs are a vital component of V2X, facilitating communication between vehicles and users, however, they have limited coverage, particularly in areas with heavy traffic. To address this challenge, we explore the use of vehicle relays to extend the RSU network, and in turn, the vehicular network coverage area. In our research, we model a two-tier heterogeneous vehicular network consisting of RSUs and vehicle relays, where the distances from vehicles to RSUs or relays follow different distributions. Furthermore, we use stochastic geometry to analyze the power-trimmed and power-matched network models, and then investigate the probability of successful decoding and network coverage. Next, we explore the relationship between vehicle relays and network coverage, particularly in terms of the optimal number of vehicle relays that can maximize the network coverage. Lastly, we validate the theoretical findings through numerical simulations.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference, and its success hinges on the quality of its content. While most readers obtain information from the platform, only a small fraction contribute to its development, and among these, an even smaller group edit articles to reflect the encyclopedia's goal of providing high-quality, reliable content successfully. Machine learning models can assist editors in identifying articles with multiple sources but poor content quality by analyzing patterns in the articles' historical development. The features of these articles are then extracted and used to differentiate between high and low quality articles, and a baseline model is established to identify articles with potential for improvement, and the effectiveness of the model is evaluated through comparative analysis and the examination of feature importance.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks, yet it relies on a labeled data source, which is often costly and impractical to obtain. We propose a novel approach to circumvent this limitation by utilizing black-box models trained on data they cannot access directly, via zero-shot knowledge distillation. We focus on models that utilize decision-based queries, and aim to replicate their training to provide simplified outputs without requiring any training data. This is achieved by formulating a zero-shot objective that targets the decision transformations utilized by the black-box model, as well as employing a variant that leverages round-trip queries to further enhance its accuracy, outperforming existing methods, up to 10 dB in mean absolute error.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays were calculated relative to $D^0 \bar{\pi}^+ \pi^- K^0_S$ and $D^0 \pi^+ \pi^- K^0_S$ $B^0_s$ decays, and were determined to be $(3.10_{-0.59}^{+0.48}\pm{0.18}\pm{0.13})\times10^{-4}$ and $(2.70_{-0.47}^{+0.35}\pm{0.15}\pm{0.12})\times10^{-4}$, respectively, with the second result representing the relative branching fraction for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with $\mathbb Z^r$-action, Mathai and Rosenberg defined the dual space as the fixed-point subalgebra. Building on their work, we generalize their result to cover twisted torus bundles. Moreover, our work provides a categorical improvement, showcasing that the mapping algebras of twisted torus bundles and their T-duals form an equivalent category with the mapping algebras of untwisted torus bundles.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be greatly improved through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, obtaining multiple sets of expert demonstrations for various tasks is often impractical. To address this challenge, co-imitation learning is proposed, which trains a co-imitator to gather environment trajectories from other agents and utilizes those data to enhance its own reinforcement learning performance. Despite its potential, co-imitation learning faces a significant obstacle: a lack of expert demonstration in its phase of other agents' training. To overcome this limitation, we've devised novel training strategies allowing a co-imitator to gather valuable, diverse agent trajectories without relying on external expertise. Moreover, we've explored how these strategies might lead to vanishing variance issues and developed methods to mitigate this problem. Our approach demonstrates that co-imitation learning can effectively consolidate and transfer skills from multiple agent trajectories to a phase where no expert involvement is required, outperforming a baseline reinforcement learning method.

This paper investigates the properties and calculations of Plain Augmentation Compression (PAC) codes, offering a systematic method to determine their length in binary representation for all cases. PAC codes are closely related to universal sets of Hamming distance and various distance-based embeddings, and some results on their existence provide insights into the attainable distances between binary and halved grids. We also examine relevant metric properties and discuss some open questions in this context.

This project addresses the complex task of tracking hands and objects within a sequence of 3D point clouds that involve both hands and one additional item. We've developed a novel approach that utilizes learning-based methods to restore hands on subsequent frames, leveraging high-resolution depth data to hand tracking. Thanks to robust optical tracking, our model achieves superior performance in discerning fine details within hand structures. We also introduce a new dataset consisting of thousands of real-world hand-object interactions with precise labeling, and attribute the cause of failures within our model to the impact of varied hand configurations and occlusions. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach with advanced applications, including hand tracking reconstruction, hand-free object manipulation, and bridging high and low resolution point clouds.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

We have created a novel, markerless robot-depth calibration-free setup that learns and accurately determines the relative positions of end-effectors and depth camera fields-of-view. Using depth images, our system can also identify and track a newly attached end-effector without the need for additional calibration. Our approach has been tested on a RobotIQ gripper and Intel RealSense depth camera, showing an average relative end-effector pose error of less than $0.5^\circ$ for roll and pitch, and less than $0.008$ for yaw. Additionally, our approach demonstrated high consistency with a maximum pose error of less than $1.5$ cm and a yaw error of less than $10^\circ$.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (treatment control pairs). Here, a general framework is developed that enables the detection of treatment interference with respect to entire units groups (treatment control groups) without targeting specific units. Under this proposed approach, a treatment interference effect is defined as there being at least one comparison pair with an average difference exceeding a predetermined threshold. Furthermore, a testing procedure is devised, and two metrics for evaluating its performance are considered: type I error and local false sign rate (LFSR). Simulations were conducted to examine the procedure's ability to control these metrics in various scenarios and demonstrate that the LFSR can be controlled at the specified level in homogeneous units scenarios, while remaining robust in heterogeneous units scenarios, with better performance observed when the number of control neighbors (K) is larger.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-annihilating dark matter within a star's core have been conducted, with particular focus on the role of the pseudoscalar interaction.  Calculations have been performed under two assumptions: one where the pseudoscalar mediator remains in the core, and another where its presence is negligible.  It's noted that interactions of the pseudoscalar with fermions can produce notable enhancements in the annihilation rate, with rates potentially rising significantly under the first assumption, while under the second, a specific neutrino emission process occurs, with annihilation rates potentially being millions of times higher than in the first scenario.  Given that neutron star cores are thought to be inhabited by non-chiral equilibrium states, the first scenario is believed to be the most accurate representation.  It's further highlighted that even in the star's initial stages, pseudoscalar interactions could lead to substantial enhancements in the annihilation emissivity, with rates potentially increasing significantly before settling into long-term equilibrium.  It's emphasized that, when considering pseudoscalar interactions, new areas of the parameter space, where dark matter can effectively be heated within a star's core, can be uncovered.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has finished its imaging sequence using the Sub-AreO Optical Element on the Magellan Baade telescope. These high-resolution images cover 10% of the sky with magnification factors between 5 and 25, enabling excellent detection of galaxy structures. To complement the main survey, the Cosmic Flow Initiation Stack (CFIS) was implemented as an additional deep layer in untargeted areas of the sky. With such impressive magnification and resolution capabilities, the UNIONS data allows for the measurement of shears across vast distances. To analyze these effects, we developed the ShapePipe pipeline and tested it on untargeted CFIS data using untargeted fields. employing the untargeted data of the Cosmic Flow Initiation Stack was integrated with additional deep deep layers in areas not targeted by the main survey. This pipeline includes a real-time measurement of the cosmic shear effect using the ShapePipe, which has confirmed that the results match those obtained by previous studies utilizing larger surveys such as the KiDS survey.

A recent discovery by Falbel reveals that Falbel-Freire type Kronecker-Weyl theorems hold for all irrational numbers, prompting questions from the authors' predecessors, specifically Huang and Li, regarding related falsetheorems and the underlying general principles. The aim of this study is to offer affirmative answers to these queries, essentially extending Falbel's original findings, and furthermore, to illustrate the wide applicability of our framework through additional examples, and to demonstrate a particularly interesting consequence: the validity of the falsetheorem is contingent upon the presence of an irrational number exhibiting a specific rational approximation property, known as the approximability condition.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling between the two magnetic sub lattices, a field applied perpendicular to the ab plane induces an intermediate regime where the system is described by the Heisenberg model with single anisotropy. Applying fields higher than 12 Tesla causes the two sub-lattices to align in an antiferromagnetic arrangement within the ab plane, which is expected to be described by the single Heisenberg model with easy-axis anisotropy. We have determined the critical field at which the system undergoes a field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless phase transition. The critical field at 2.4 GHz, 2019 \pm 16 Tesla, closely matches theoretical predictions of 205 Tesla. 2019 \pm 16 Tesla, through an anisotropy model, is derived from the critical field.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and the muon anomaly, offering a right-handed theta angle that compensates for neutrino mass terms. This setup allows for the generation of dark matter through both axion and sterile neutrino abundance, achieved through an oscillation between the two. As a result, the model predicts sub-GeV mass ranges for both the axion and sterile neutrino, within limits imposed by stellar evolution and cosmic microwave background analysis. The compatibility of the model with collider searches for sterile neutrinos is also examined.

This study improves the known limit on how quickly the stabilizer rank of a specific type of quantum state decreases with its size. For a certain function of multiple quantum bits, this study shows the growth is bounded above by the function to the power of $d$ minus 1. This result is the tightest limit established so far, with implications that past research on specific polynomial and Clifford circuits could be scaled up in depth. This improvement also deepens the understanding of how complex quantum circuits can be approximated classically.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, investigating its 
temperature behavior along with critical and saddle points through complex analysis.
Furthermore, visual representations of energy density and deceleration parameters 
are provided to examine the universe's evolution through simple and complicated 
formulations of the quintessence model.
We utilize mathematical techniques such as the Residue Theorem and argue for the 
feasibility of applying complex analysis in studying holographic dark energy under 
various models to examine the universe's early evolution.

Between October 2019 and January 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique multi-object spectroscopy on 4 $K2$ transit-monitoring plates. Each plate is designed to capture 1024 objects, with 40 objects per field, across eight different exposures per object. The data retrieved from these observations shows a rich data source, where the LAMOST's$\sim$2500 objects per plate is further increased by approximately 4 times with re-observations. The collected data has shown significant APOGEE matches with about 48%, where those matches exhibit enhanced signal strength. Analyzing MWDJ4437-4778's light curves across four plates revealed three distinct flaring events. Flare-related current patterns were successfully predicted using random forest (RF) and support vector machine (SVM) models through field matching and APOGEE selection. The LAMOST's$K2$ project now contributes valuable data towards increasing our knowledge of stellar phenomena, especially those related to magnetic activity across various stellar types.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in portable devices, incorporating an SRAM-based TRNG would be both space-efficient and cost-effective. Notwithstanding, the existing SRAM-based TRNG research primarily relies on the faulty rows of the SRAM array, given that manufacturing defects are unpredictable. Consequently, the efficacy of these TRNGs is constrained by the scarcity of faulty rows. In this paper, we present a novel SRAM-based TRNG that leverages the SRAM cell's supply voltage to generate true random numbers, leveraging the inherent process variations. By utilizing a single supply voltage underscaling technique and incorporating a simple, on-the-fly post-processing module, we demonstrate that high-quality random numbers can be generated at speeds exceeding 1 kbits/s. Our proposed TRNG, denoted as TuRaN, undergoes a comprehensive evaluation, and the results show its superiority to existing SRAM-based TRNG research in terms of entropy, randomness, and miniaturization.

A preliminary design and simulation of single-electron resistive switches has been developed, utilizing Lennard-Jones molecules as the active element. These molecular residues are set within a circuit that includes quantum point contacts for regulation, exhibiting a notable increase in resistance when the quantum point contacts are partially closed. Notably, uncharged noise particles are also present in the system, residing within an adjacent metal trap that can be filled or emptied by controlled charges. Studies have revealed that the noise's insertion into or removal from the metal trap causes a sudden increase in the switches' resistance, exhibiting properties suitable for single-electron memory applications.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. However, the practical implementation of loop-tree duality for multi-loop processes is hindered due to the presence of loop subgraphs. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel technique that enables the representation of loop subgraphs. When combined with standard loop-tree duality and hexagon function basis properties, this approach facilitates the numerical evaluation of multi-loop Feynman integrals. Using this technique, we successfully compute the three-loop massless self-energy and the finite parts of the two-loop scalar integrals with five and six propagators.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related but distinct approach involving the use of resolvent kernels and connections to orthogonal polutes was previously done by S. L. Barry et al. We examine the continuous two-state quantum walk as a limiting case of the discrete version and show that the expansion formula can be derived from its Green's function, a finding consistent with a broader principle stated in a separate study.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This study investigates the optical properties of a setup consisting of a $q$-deformed cavity coupled to an input field and a drugged drum, influenced by thermal noise. By introducing the Gross-Pitaevskii equation to model the interaction between the cavity field and the damping rate, and employing the input-output theory, we examine the impact of $q$-deformation and noise on optical transparency and slow light. We demonstrate that $q$-deformation enhances the transparency window of the system and that under specific conditions, the transparency and acceleration of light can be regulated. However, $q$-deformation has a limit, beyond which the optical properties revert to conventional behavior.

In a previous study, I developed a model for the two rotors framework, where the negative scissors state is composed of two excitation types: one has R-negative parity and the other has R-positive parity. The scissors states with different R-parities exhibit unique characteristics, and their mixing rations differ, and their intensity ratios depend on specific factors, which vary for each R-parity. In this work, I apply my model to predict properties of negative scissors states with R-negative and R-positive parity, and compare these predictions with experimental observations for certain double-core nuclei. Furthermore, I utilize my model to analyze the R-parity and mixing ration of the scissors states in $^{162}$Dy, $^{164}$Gd, and $^{166}$Er and determine how the R-negative and R-positive scissors modes' intensity ratios rely on the R-parity.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different insulating phases emerge from the same initial high-symmetry state, each exhibiting a distinct combination of spin and orbital order. We consider the role of the substrate in breaking the orbital degeneracy and inducing this order. When the interaction with the substrate is weak or preferentially affects the orbital angular momentum, we observe ordered arrangements of orbitals coexisting with disordered spins at low temperatures, resulting in two distinct ordered phases of orbitals as the temperature changes. Conversely, if the substrate interaction is strong and overrides electron-electron interactions, the system displays simultaneous ordering of orbits and spins at a higher temperature, leading to a greater number of ordered phases characterized by the arrangements of orbits and local magnetic moments.
